stimuli.title: The Second Hand
stimuli.text:
**1** The bell over the door of Ramos Watch Repair rang only a few times on a Saturday, and Mateo had learned to hear it even through the ticking. There were forty clocks on the walls of his great-uncle's shop, and each one kept a slightly different time, so the room never fell silent. Tio Ramon said the noise helped him think. Mateo said it gave him a headache, but he came every Saturday anyway, because his mother had arranged it and because Tio Ramon paid him in cash.

**2** That morning a woman in a nurse's uniform set a pocket watch on the counter. The crystal was cracked and the hands had stopped at twenty past four. "It was my father's," she said. "I dropped it on the hospital stairs. I know it's probably hopeless."

**3** Mateo felt his face grow warm. He took the watch carefully, as if it might break further in his hands, and he did not look at her.

**4** He had been nine the summer he broke his grandfather's watch. It had been lying on the kitchen table, gold and heavy, and he had only wanted to see whether it would spin like a top. It spun. Then it skated off the edge and struck the tile floor. The glass had split into a star.

**5** No one had seen. Mateo had wrapped the watch in a sock and pushed it to the back of his desk drawer, and when his grandfather searched the house for it that evening, Mateo searched too, opening cabinets he knew were empty. His grandfather never found it. He died two winters later, and the watch was still in the drawer.

**6** Mateo had never told anyone. Some nights he still took the sock out and held the watch without unwrapping it.

**7** "Mateo." Tio Ramon was standing beside him. "Are you going to write the ticket, or are you going to stare at it?"

**8** Mateo wrote the ticket. After the woman left, his uncle unscrewed the back of the watch and laid the tiny parts on a white cloth in rows, the way a surgeon might lay out instruments. He worked without hurrying. When a spring jumped from his tweezers and vanished, he did not mutter, as Mateo would have. He simply turned off the fan, waited for the air to go still, and found the spring with a magnet.

**9** "How do you know it can be fixed?" Mateo asked.

**10** "I don't," Tio Ramon said. "Nobody knows until they open it up. Most things people think are ruined are only waiting for someone to look at them properly."

**11** By closing time the nurse's watch was ticking. Mateo watched the second hand sweep around once, twice. Then he heard himself say, "I have one, too. A watch. It's been broken for six years."

**12** His uncle did not ask how it had broken. He only took a fresh white cloth from the drawer and spread it on the bench between them.

**13** "Bring it next Saturday," he said. "You can do the unscrewing."

stimuli.title: Let the Night Be Dark
stimuli.text:
**1** Step outside in the center of almost any Texas city after sunset and look up. If you can count more than a handful of stars, you are lucky. The sky above most of our towns glows a dull orange, lit not by the moon but by millions of bulbs pointed in the wrong direction. Our cities should require outdoor lights to be shielded and aimed downward, and they should turn off lights that no one needs.

**2** The first reason is the simplest: wasted light is wasted money. A bulb that shines sideways into a neighbor's bedroom or straight up into the sky lights nothing that anyone is using. Every city pays to power its streetlights, and every business pays to light its parking lot. When a fixture throws much of its light where it is not wanted, a share of that bill buys nothing at all.

**3** The second reason flies over our heads every spring and fall. Texas lies under one of the great routes that migrating birds follow between North and South America, and most songbirds make the journey at night. Bright lights can pull these birds off course. Some circle lit buildings until they are exhausted; others strike windows they cannot see. A friend of mine who volunteers with a bird group walks downtown sidewalks at dawn during migration. She told me she once filled a shoebox with warblers before seven in the morning. None of them had to die.

**4** Critics sometimes say that people like me want to turn off every streetlight and leave the streets in darkness. No one is proposing that. Light at night has real uses. A well-lit crosswalk protects people on foot, and a lit doorway helps a family find their way home. I agree that safety matters. But a shielded fixture that points down puts more light on the sidewalk, not less, because none of it is lost to the sky. Glare from an unshielded bulb can even make it harder to see, as anyone who has squinted into a floodlight knows.

**5** The changes I am asking for are not complicated. Cities can require new outdoor fixtures to be fully shielded. They can dim or switch off lights on empty ball fields and office lots after midnight. Homeowners can replace a bare porch bulb with one that has a hood. None of these steps requires us to give up the light we use. They only ask us to stop paying for the light we do not.

**6** People lived under a sky full of stars for almost all of human history. We do not have to choose between safe streets and a dark sky. With a few sensible rules, our children could step outside on a clear night and see the Milky Way from their own front yards.

stimuli.title: Paired selections: "Learning the River" and "The Dock"
stimuli.text:
**Selection 1: Learning the River**

The river did not care that I was eight.

It moved the way it always moved,

brown and patient, sliding past the willows

as if it had somewhere better to be.

My brother stood in it up to his chest

and held out both his hands.

I stood on the bank and counted

every reason not to:

the cold, the current, the fish I could not see.

He did not argue. He only waited,

and the river waited with him.

When I finally stepped in, the water

closed around my knees like a fist,

then loosened, then let me go.

Now I am the one standing in the river.

Now I am the one who waits.

**Selection 2: The Dock**

**1** My father taught me to swim the summer I turned eleven, which was late, and both of us knew it. Every other kid at the lake could already swim to the floating dock and back. I could stand in water up to my waist and pretend I had no interest in going farther.

**2** Our lessons happened after dinner, when the beach had emptied. My father did not believe in shouting instructions from the shore. He waded out with me and stayed beside me, close enough to touch, for every single stroke. When I panicked and swallowed water, he did not tell me to calm down. He told me about the summer he had nearly drowned in a stock tank in West Texas, and how his own father had pulled him out by the collar of his shirt.

**3** "You were scared, too?" I asked.

**4** "I was terrified," he said. "I still don't like deep water. That's why I want you to be good at it."

**5** It had never occurred to me that my father could be afraid of anything. That evening, our nightly tête-à-tête at the end of the dock lasted until the mosquitoes drove us inside, and I asked him questions I had never thought to ask before.

**6** By August I could swim to the floating dock. I remember climbing the ladder and turning around to wave, expecting to see him watching from the beach. Instead he was in the water a few yards behind me, treading quietly, as he had been the whole way. It was the most embarrassing and the most comforting thing he ever did.

stimuli.title: A student's draft: Bats on the Night Shift
stimuli.text:
(1) Every evening from spring through fall, huge numbers of Mexican free-tailed bats pour out of caves and from under bridges across Texas. (2) Bats are interesting. (3) Some of the largest bat colonies in the world live in the state. (4) One of these colonies spends its summers in Bracken Cave near San Antonio. (5) Another colony roosts under the Congress Avenue Bridge in Austin, where crowds gather to watch them leave at dusk.

(6) Once they are in the air, the bats get to work. (7) They hunt flying insects, and many of those insects are moths whose young feed on crops such as corn and cotton. (8) A bat can eat a large share of its own weight in insects in a single night. (9) Some people are afraid of bats because of scary movies. (10) Farmers who have bats nearby may need to spray fewer chemicals on their fields.

(11) Bats face serious threats. (12) Caves are disturbed by visitors, and the places bats roost are sometimes destroyed. (13) People can protect bats by leaving roosts alone and by supporting groups that protect caves. (14) Bats help us, and we should do stuff for them.

stimuli.title: A student's draft: a letter about a crosswalk
stimuli.text:
Dear Council Member Alvarez:

(1) I am a ninth-grade student at Rio Vista High School, and I am writing to ask the city to add a marked crosswalk on Mesquite Road in front of our school. (2) Right now, students who live in the neighborhood across the road have no safe place to cross. (3) The nearest traffic light is almost half a mile away.

(4) Most students do not walk to the light. (5) Instead, they dart across four lanes of traffic during the morning rush. (6) Drivers on Mesquite Road often go faster than the posted limit. (7) Last month a classmate of mine was nearly hit by a pickup truck while she was crossing. (8) Running across the road, her backpack fell open and spilled into the lane.

(9) A crosswalk with flashing lights would remind drivers to slow down, make students visible, and it would give families a safe route to school. (10) Our student council has collected more than three hundred signatures from students and parents who support the idea.

(11) This thing is a really big deal, so please do something about it soon. (12) Thank you for your time and for your service to our community.

Sincerely,

Daniela Ortiz

stimuli.title: A student's draft: Saturday at the Market
stimuli.text:
(1) The summer before ninth grade, I worked every Saturday at my aunt's booth at the farmers market in our town. (2) We sold peaches, tomatoes, and jars of honey from her bees. (3) I had to wake up at five o'clock, I was usually still half asleep when we loaded the truck.

(4) The market opened at seven. (5) By then, farmers who sell there had to set up his own tables and shade tents. (6) My aunt showed me how to stack the peaches so that the bruised ones stayed on the bottom. (7) She also taught me a few words of spanish so that I could greet the customers who stopped by her booth.

(8) At first, I hated talking to strangers. (9) By the end of June, though, I knew the regular customers by name, and some of them ask for me when they arrived. (10) I learned that a friendly greeting could make someone come back the next week. (11) I also learned that I could recieve a compliment without turning red.

stimuli.title: A student's draft: The Wall That Saved a City
stimuli.text:
(1) On September 8, 1900, a powerful hurricane struck the island city of Galveston, Texas. (2) Wind and a huge storm surge destroyed thousands of buildings. (3) The storm remains the deadliest natural disaster in the history of the United States.

(4) After the storm, the people of Galveston had to decide whether to rebuild. (5) They chose to fight back against the sea. (6) Two years later, work began on a concrete seawall along the shore facing the Gulf. (7) At the same time. (8) Workers pumped sand under the city to raise the ground behind the wall.

(9) The project was enormous homes, churches, and even water pipes had to be lifted while the sand was poured beneath them. (10) The wall was built by thousands of workers over many years. (11) In later storms, the wall protected the city from much of the damage it suffered in 1900.

(12) Today, the seawall is a popular place to: walk, ride bikes, and watch the waves. (13) Most visitors do not realize that they are standing on one of the countrys great engineering projects.

stimuli.title: The Understudy
stimuli.text:
*CHARACTERS: NOELLE, fifteen; GRACE, her older sister, eighteen; MR. PARK, the drama teacher.*

*The stage of a high school auditorium, late afternoon. A single work light. NOELLE sits on the edge of the stage, a script in her lap. GRACE enters from the back of the house carrying two cups of lemonade.*

**GRACE:** Mom said you'd still be here. They posted the cast list an hour ago.

**NOELLE:** I know. I read it. I'm the understudy.

**GRACE:** *(sitting beside her)* The understudy for the lead. That's not nothing.

**NOELLE:** It's exactly nothing. I learn every line, I go to every rehearsal, and then I sit in the wings and watch Priya do it. *(to the audience)* Grace was the lead in every play she ever tried out for. She doesn't know what it is to wait.

**GRACE:** When I was a freshman, I didn't get cast at all. Did you know that?

**NOELLE:** You never told me that.

**GRACE:** I never told anyone. I told Mom the play was boring and I'd decided not to try out. *(She laughs.)* I painted sets instead. I spent the whole spring covered in blue paint.

*MR. PARK enters from stage left, reading a phone. He does not see the girls at first.*

**MR. PARK:** *(into the phone)* No, I understand. Feel better. We'll manage. *(He hangs up, then notices NOELLE.)* Noelle. Good. You're still here.

**NOELLE:** I was just leaving.

**MR. PARK:** How well do you know the second act?

**NOELLE:** *(standing slowly)* Every word. Why?

**MR. PARK:** Because Priya's family is moving to Houston at the end of the month, and she just told me she won't be here for opening night. *(pause)* I'd like to see you run the second act tomorrow. Bring your script, though I doubt you'll need it.

*He exits. NOELLE stares after him. GRACE holds out the second cup of lemonade.*

**GRACE:** That's not nothing, either.

**NOELLE:** *(taking the cup, quietly)* I was going to quit tonight. I had the email written.

**GRACE:** I know. *(beat)* Mom said that, too.

*Lights fade.*

stimuli.title: Making Room for the Ocelot
stimuli.text:
**1** In the thick brush of South Texas lives a wild cat that most Texans have never seen. The ocelot is about twice the size of a house cat, with a coat of black spots and stripes on gold fur. It hunts at night and spends its days hidden in dense thorny shrubs. Ocelots once ranged across much of South and Central Texas. Today only a small number are known to breed in the United States, all in the southern tip of the state, and the species is listed as endangered. Saving the ocelot depends on two things: protecting the brush it needs and helping it travel safely between the patches that are left.

**Losing Ground**

**2** Ocelots need cover. They avoid open ground, where they are easy to see, and they rarely cross wide fields. Over the past century most of the native brush in the Rio Grande Valley was cleared for farms, towns and roads. The remaining brush is broken into small, separate pieces. Each piece may be large enough for only one or two cats, and young ocelots that leave home to find their own territory must cross open land to reach another patch.

**Danger on the Road**

**3** That crossing is where many ocelots die. Vehicle strikes are one of the leading known causes of death for ocelots in Texas. A road through brush country cuts a cat's territory in two, and a young male searching for a home may have to cross several highways in a single night.

**4** To reduce these deaths, engineers have built wildlife crossings: tunnels and culverts under highways, paired with fences that guide animals toward them. Cameras placed in the tunnels have recorded ocelots, bobcats and many other animals using them. A crossing works only if it connects brush to brush, so biologists study where cats actually travel before a site is chosen.

**Room to Grow**

**5** Crossings cannot help if there is nowhere for the cats to go. Wildlife refuges in the Valley have planted native shrubs on old farm fields, and some private landowners have agreed to leave brush standing on their ranches. Because most land in Texas is privately owned, these agreements matter. A ranch that keeps a strip of thick brush along a fence line can link two patches that were once cut off from each other.

**6** Brush planted today will take years to grow thick enough for an ocelot to hide in. The people working to save the cat know that their efforts may not show results for a long time. Still, each new crossing and each acre of restored brush gives a young ocelot one more safe path through the place its ancestors once ruled.

stimuli.title: Paired selections: "Monarchs, October" and "A Highway for Butterflies"
stimuli.text:
**Selection 1: Monarchs, October**

They come through in the afternoon,

a few, then dozens, then more than I can count,

orange sparks drifting south above the parking lot

as if someone had shaken out a fire.

None of them has made this trip before.

None of them will make it twice.

And still they know the way, the way

a song knows where it ends.

I stand by my car with my keys in my hand

and forget, for a minute, where I was going.

**Selection 2: A Highway for Butterflies**

**1** Each fall, millions of monarch butterflies leave the northern United States and Canada and fly to the mountains of central Mexico, where they spend the winter clustered on fir trees. For many of them, the route passes through Texas. In spring, their offspring begin the trip north again. No single butterfly completes the whole cycle; it takes several generations.

**2** Along the way, monarchs depend on two kinds of plants. Adults drink nectar from flowers for the energy they need to fly. Caterpillars eat only milkweed, so a female monarch must find milkweed plants on which to lay her eggs. Where milkweed and wildflowers have disappeared, monarchs have fewer places to stop and breed.

**3** Because Interstate 35 runs north and south through the center of the monarch's route, several states along the highway have agreed to plant milkweed and native flowers on the land beside it. Highway workers have also changed when and how often they mow, so that flowers have time to bloom. These strips of roadside habitat cost little and can stretch for hundreds of miles.

**4** Anyone can help. A pot of milkweed on a balcony or a patch of native flowers in a schoolyard can give a passing monarch a place to rest. Scientists say that many small gardens, added together, can matter as much as a single large one.

stimuli.title: A student's draft: Every Student Should Learn to Cook
stimuli.text:
(1) Most high school students can use a phone to order dinner in seconds. (2) Far fewer could make dinner themselves. (3) Our school should require every student to take a basic cooking class before graduation.

(4) Cooking is a skill people use for the rest of their lives. (5) Students who know how to cook can save money by preparing meals at home instead of buying them. (6) They can also make healthier choices, because they control what goes into their food. (7) My older brother learned to cook in college. (8) Also, a cooking class teaches math and science, such as measuring ingredients and understanding how heat changes food.

(9) Some people argue that there is no room in the schedule for another required class. (10) A cooking class could take the place of one semester of an elective. (11) Students would still have time for other subjects.

(12) A cooking class gives students something they can use every single day. (13) Learning to cook is good and our school should do it.

stimuli.title: A student's draft: The Dress in the Closet
stimuli.text:
(1) In the back of my grandmother's closet hangs a pale yellow dress wrapped in plastic. (2) She wore it to her quinceañera in 1974, in a small town outside Laredo. (3) For most of my childhood, I thought it was just an old dress.

(4) Last spring, I asked her about it. (5) She unzipped the plastic and told me the story. (6) Her mother had sewn the dress by hand over three months, working at night after her shifts at a laundry. (7) The fabric had cost more in a whole year than the family usually spent on clothes. (8) The dress was very nice.

(9) My grandmother let me try it on. (10) It fit almost perfectly. (11) When I looked in the mirror, I thought about my great-grandmother bent over her sewing machine. (12) She was tired. (13) She kept working anyway.

(14) I used to think the dress was just old. (15) Now I know it holds a story about sacrifice and love.

stimuli.title: A student's draft: The Chisholm Trail
stimuli.text:
(1) After the Civil War, Texas had millions of longhorn cattle and very few buyers. (2) In the cities of the North, beef was scarce and prices were high. (3) Texas ranchers realized that if they could get their cattle to a railroad, they could sell them for far more than they were worth at home.

(4) The answer was the cattle drive. (5) Cowboys drove herds of thousands of cattle north to railroad towns in Kansas. (6) Such as Abilene. (7) The most famous route was the Chisholm Trail, named for a trader who had used part of the path before the drives began.

(8) A drive could take two or three months. (9) The cowboys crossed rivers, the weather could be dangerous, and stampedes. (10) Each night, the cowboys take turns watching the herd.

(11) By the end of the 1880s, railroads had reached texas, and the long drives came to an end. (12) In less than twenty years, though, the trail had become a lasting part of the history of the American west.

stimuli.title: A student's draft: an email to a librarian
stimuli.text:
Dear Ms. Hughes,

(1) My name is Tomas Reyes, and I am the president of the Chess Club at Lakeview high school. (2) I am writing to ask whether our club could use the library study room on Thursday afternoons. (3) Our club meets after school, we need a quiet place to play.

(4) Right now we meet in the cafeteria. (5) It is often loud because other clubs are using it at the same time. (6) Last week, our members have to stop a game three times because of the noise. (7) The study room, which has a large table and a door that closes would be ideal.

(8) We would follow all library rules and leave the room as we found it. (9) We would be happy to bring our own boards and pieces; so nothing in the library would be used. (10) We could also invite students who visit the library to join us. (11) The club has ten members right now, and we are hoping to grow.

(12) Thank you for considering our request. (13) I look forward to hearing from you.

Sincerely,

Tomas Reyes

stimuli.title: Tryouts
stimuli.text:
**1** The cross-country coach posted the varsity list on the gym door at 3:15, and by 3:16 Ana knew she was not on it. Her name was third on the junior varsity list, right below Celeste Moreno's, which somehow made it worse.

**2** Celeste had joined the team in August. She had never run a race before, and on the first day she had stopped to walk twice in the first mile. Ana had run every summer since sixth grade, before the sun came up, while her little brothers slept. She had a notebook with every split she had ever recorded.

**3** "Congratulations," Celeste said, appearing beside her. "We're both JV. We can train together."

**4** Ana made her mouth smile. "Sure," she said, and she walked to the parking lot without stretching.

**5** That night she opened the notebook and read it from the beginning. The early pages were crowded with times, each one a few seconds faster than the last. The recent pages were different. The numbers had stopped dropping in July. Beside one entry, in handwriting she barely remembered, she had written "legs heavy, ran anyway." Beside another, "skipped hills, too hot." She had been running more than anyone, she realized, but she had stopped paying attention to how.

**6** On Monday she found Celeste at the bottom of the long hill behind the school, staring up at it.

**7** "I hate this hill," Celeste said.

**8** "Me too," Ana said. She opened the notebook to a clean page and wrote the date at the top. "Let's time it."

stimuli.title: Inheritance
stimuli.text:
My grandfather left me nothing you could hold:

no watch, no ring, no box of letters tied with string.

He left the way he whistled through his teeth

when the bread was rising,

the way he tested a melon with his thumb

and said, *not yet, not yet.*

He left me the word *patience*,

though he never said it once.

Some mornings I catch myself

pressing a melon at the market,

whistling through my teeth,

and the whole crowded aisle goes quiet,

and there he is.

stimuli.title: Phones in Class: Teach, Don't Ban
stimuli.text:
**1** Several school districts have recently banned students from carrying phones during the school day. The goal is understandable: phones can distract students and pull their attention away from lessons. But a total ban treats a skill problem as a discipline problem. Instead of locking phones away, schools should teach students when and how to use them.

**2** Consider what students will face after graduation. Almost every job, college class and household now depends on phones and similar devices. An adult who cannot put a phone down during a meeting will struggle at work, and no employer will lock that phone in a pouch. If high school is meant to prepare young people for adult life, it should help them practice self-control, not remove the need for it.

**3** Phones can also be useful learning tools. A student can photograph a whiteboard full of notes, record a lab result or look up a word in a dictionary in seconds. Teachers in many classrooms already use phones for quick quizzes and polls. A ban takes these tools away from every student because some misuse them.

**4** Supporters of bans point out that phones are designed to grab attention, and that teenagers find them hard to resist. That is true, and it is exactly why schools should not ignore the problem. Clear rules, such as phones face down on the desk unless the teacher asks for them, give students practice in resisting distraction while an adult is there to help.

**5** Some will say that teaching self-control takes time teachers do not have. But schools already make time to teach students how to write an email and how to stay safe online. Learning to manage a phone belongs on the same list.

**6** A ban may make classrooms quieter for a year. Teaching students to manage their phones will help them for the rest of their lives.

stimuli.title: The River Under the Hills
stimuli.text:
**1** Beneath the Texas Hill Country lies a hidden reservoir. The Edwards Aquifer is not an underground lake but a vast layer of limestone riddled with cracks, channels and caves, all filled with water. Millions of people in and around San Antonio depend on it for drinking water, and farmers and ranchers draw on it to grow crops and raise livestock.

**How Water Gets In**

**2** The aquifer is filled, or recharged, in a particular area. North and west of San Antonio, the limestone rises to the surface. When rain falls there, or when creeks flow across the exposed rock, water sinks through the cracks and into the aquifer below. This region is called the recharge zone. Because water enters the aquifer so quickly there, anything spilled on the ground in the recharge zone can reach the water supply with little filtering.

**How Water Gets Out**

**3** Water leaves the aquifer in two ways. People pump it out through wells, and it flows out naturally through springs. Some of the largest springs in Texas, including those at San Marcos and New Braunfels, are fed by the Edwards. These springs are home to plants and animals found nowhere else in the world, such as a small blind salamander that lives in the underground water.

**Balancing the Supply**

**4** During a drought, less water enters the aquifer while people pump more of it for lawns and crops. If the water level falls too far, the springs can slow to a trickle, threatening the animals that live in them. For that reason, the region has rules that limit pumping when water levels drop. Cities ask residents to water their lawns less often, and some farmers are paid to leave fields unwatered during the driest years.

**5** The Edwards Aquifer cannot be seen from the highway, but it shapes life above it every day. Protecting it means paying attention to what happens on the surface, from a rain shower in the hills to a sprinkler in a front yard.

stimuli.title: The Last Shift
stimuli.text:
*A small family restaurant at closing time. Chairs are stacked on most of the tables. ABUELA LUPE, seventy, wipes the counter. Her grandson DIEGO, sixteen, sweeps the floor with his earbuds in.*

**LUPE:** Diego. *(He does not hear.)* Diego!

**DIEGO:** *(pulling out one earbud)* What?

**LUPE:** You missed the corner. You always miss the corner.

**DIEGO:** Nobody looks at the corner, Abuela.

**LUPE:** I look at the corner. *(She sets down her rag.)* Forty-one years I have looked at that corner.

*DIEGO sweeps the corner, rolling his eyes. LUPE watches him, then sits heavily at the one table with no chairs on it.*

**LUPE:** The man from the bank came again today.

**DIEGO:** *(stopping)* The one who wants to buy the building?

**LUPE:** He says the offer is good. He says I could rest. *(She laughs a little.)* As if I know how to rest.

**DIEGO:** *(setting the broom against the wall, taking out the other earbud)* Are you going to sell?

**LUPE:** Your mother thinks I should. My knees think I should. *(pause)* I wanted to know what you think.

*DIEGO looks around the room: the stacked chairs, the photographs on the wall, the corner he just swept.*

**DIEGO:** I think somebody has to keep looking at the corner.

*LUPE looks at him for a long moment. Then she picks up her rag again.*

**LUPE:** Tomorrow, come at six. I'll show you how to make the salsa.

*Lights fade.*

stimuli.title: My Uncle's Kitchen
stimuli.text:
**1** My uncle Felipe ran a small catering business out of a rented kitchen near downtown Corpus Christi, and the summer I turned fifteen, he hired me. I suspect my mother had asked him to, though neither of them ever admitted it.

**2** He gave me carte blanche on my first day, which turned out to mean that no one would tell me what to do. I spent the morning wandering between stations, trying to look busy. By noon I had broken a bowl, burned a tray of tortillas and learned more words in kitchen slang than I had in a year of Spanish class.

**3** The kitchen was a frenzy every afternoon. Orders arrived faster than anyone could read them, pans clattered and the cooks shouted the times left on each dish. Yet in the middle of the noise my uncle moved slowly, almost lazily, tasting a sauce here and adjusting a burner there. Only later did I understand that his calm was deliberate. A cook who panics burns things, he told me. A cook who is calm has time to fix them.

**4** By August I had my own station, rolling dough for empanadas. I was not fast, but I was consistent, and my uncle said consistency was the whole secret of the business. A customer who orders the same dish twice expects it to taste the same, and a cook who cannot repeat a success has only been lucky.

**5** On my last day he handed me an envelope with my pay and a recipe card in his crooked handwriting. "Bon appetit," he said, grinning, because he knew I had been teased all summer for the one French phrase I knew. The card had his empanada recipe on it, the one he had never written down for anyone. I still have it, stained with oil, in the back of my wallet.

stimuli.title: A student's draft: Wings Over Sweetwater
stimuli.text:
(1) During World War II, the United States needed pilots to fly military planes from factories to air bases. (2) Many male pilots were fighting overseas. (3) The answer came from an unexpected group of people.

(4) In 1943, the Army began training women pilots at Avenger Field in Sweetwater, Texas. (5) These women became known as the Women Airforce Service Pilots, or WASP. (6) More than a thousand women earned their wings. (7) They flew planes across the country, tested repaired aircraft, and towed targets so that gunners on the ground could practice. (8) Sweetwater is a small town in West Texas.

(9) The WASP were not treated as members of the military. (10) When the program ended in 1944, the women had to pay their own way home. (11) It took until 1977 for Congress to recognize them as veterans.

(12) Today, a museum at Avenger Field tells their story. (13) The WASP did something.

stimuli.title: A student's draft: Our Town Needs a Skate Park
stimuli.text:
(1) Every afternoon, skateboarders in our town practice in the parking lot behind the grocery store. (2) The store manager has asked them to leave many times, and police officers have been called twice this year. (3) Skateboarders need a better place to go.

(4) A public skate park would give young people a safe place to be active. (5) Skating in a parking lot means dodging cars and shoppers. (6) In a park, skaters could practice on smooth ramps designed for the sport. (7) Skateboarding became an Olympic sport in 2021.

(8) A skate park would also help local businesses. (9) The grocery store would no longer have skaters messing around in its lot. (10) Families who visit the park might stop at nearby restaurants.

(11) Some residents worry about the cost. (12) The city could apply for grants that help towns build parks, and local businesses could sponsor ramps. (13) A skate park is a good idea.

stimuli.title: A student's draft: The Storm
stimuli.text:
(1) The power went out at 9:40, just as the wind began to howl. (2) Marisol and her little brother Teo sat on the living room floor with a flashlight between them. (3) Rain hit the windows. (4) It was loud. (5) Their parents were still at work across town.

(6) Teo started to cry. (7) Marisol didn't know what to do at first. (8) Then she remembered how their grandmother used to tell stories during storms. (9) She pointed the flashlight at the ceiling and made a shadow bird with her hands. (10) Teo stopped crying and watched.

(11) Marisol told him a story about a bird who flew through a storm to find its nest. (12) Teo fell asleep with his head on her shoulder. (13) The storm ended. (14) Marisol felt proud.

(15) When their parents finally came home, they found both children asleep on the floor.

stimuli.title: A student's draft: Learning to Sign
stimuli.text:
(1) When my cousin Lily was born deaf, my whole family decided to learn american sign language. (2) I was twelve, and I thought it would be easy. (3) I was wrong.

(4) Our teacher, a woman named Mrs. Okafor came to my aunt's house every Tuesday evening. (5) She showed us that signing is not just spelling words with your fingers. (6) Facial expressions and the direction of your hands changes the meaning of a sign. (7) My brother and me practiced every night at the dinner table.

(8) The hardest part was learning to watch instead of listen. (9) In a spoken conversation, I could look away and still follow along. (10) In ASL, looking away means missing the whole sentence.

(11) Lily is four now, and she signs faster than any of us. (12) Last month she corrected my sign for butterfly, she laughed when I got it wrong. (13) I didn't mind. (14) She is the best teacher I have ever had, and I am still learning the alphabet of a languege that has changed my family.

stimuli.title: A student's draft: a letter to the editor
stimuli.text:
To the Editor:

(1) I am writing about the decision to close the Westside Library branch on Saturdays. (2) The library board say the change will save money. (3) However, the change will hurt the students and working families who depends on the library the most.

(4) Many students in our neighborhood do not have internet at home. (5) On weekdays they are in school until four o'clock, and the library closes at six. (6) Saturday is the only full day the computers can be used by them. (7) Last year, student's used the Saturday computer lab more than any other group.

(8) Working parents feel the loss too. (9) Many of them can only bring there children to story time on weekends. (10) Without saturday hours, those families will have nowhere to go.

(11) I urge the board to find savings elsewhere. (12) For example the library could close an hour earlier on Mondays, when fewer people visit. (13) The Westside Library has served this neighborhood for fifty years it should keep serving everyone.

Sincerely,

Rosa Delgado

stimuli.title: A student's draft: The Story of the Bluebonnet
stimuli.text:
(1) Every spring, roadsides across Texas turn blue with bluebonnets. (2) The flower was named the state flower of Texas in 1901. (3) Bluebonnets are a kind of lupine a plant in the pea family.

(4) Bluebonnets grow from seeds that fall to the ground in late spring. (5) The seeds have hard outer shells. (6) Some seeds sprout the next year, but others wait several years before they grows. (7) This helps the plant servive droughts.

(8) Many Texans have a tradition. (9) Each spring, families travel to the hill country to take photographs in fields of bluebonnets. (10) Visitors are asked to be careful not to trample the plants, because a crushed plant cannot make seeds.

(11) Bluebonnets need three things to thrive, sunlight, well-drained soil, and very little fertilizer. (12) Because they need so little care. (13) They are a favorite of gardeners who want to plant native flowers.

questions.stem: How do paragraphs 4 through 6 contribute to the development of the story?
options: They describe how Tio Ramon came to own the shop
They show how Mateo first learned to repair watches
They reveal what happened to the nurse's father
They explain why the nurse's watch upsets Mateo
questions.explanation: Paragraphs 4 through 6 are a flashback to the summer Mateo broke and hid his grandfather's watch, which explains why he blushes and cannot look at the nurse. Nothing in them shows Mateo learning repair; that begins later, with his uncle.

questions.stem: How does Tio Ramon's reaction to the lost spring in paragraph 8 help develop Mateo's character?
options: It hints that Mateo is afraid of his uncle's temper
It proves that Mateo wants to own the shop someday
It shows that Mateo is more careful than his uncle
It sets Mateo's impatience against his uncle's calm
questions.explanation: The narrator says Tio Ramon did not mutter "as Mateo would have," so the uncle works as a foil whose patience shows Mateo's impatience. Nothing suggests the uncle has a temper.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses a theme of the story?
options: Old objects matter more than the people who own them
Facing a hidden mistake can be the start of repair
Hard work is the only way to earn an adult's respect
A secret kept long enough eventually stops mattering
questions.explanation: Mateo's broken watch stays hidden for six years, and the story ends with him telling his uncle and being invited to fix it, which ties honesty about a mistake to repair. The secret clearly still matters to Mateo, who holds the watch some nights.

questions.stem: How does the setting of the shop influence the theme of the story?
options: Its noisy clocks make Mateo want to leave the job
Its old tools and clocks show that watch repair is dying out
Its location in a busy city keeps customers away
Its slow, careful work models the patience repair takes
questions.explanation: The shop is a place where things are taken apart and fixed without hurrying, the same patience the story suggests Mateo needs to face his own broken watch. The ticking annoys Mateo, but he keeps coming back, so the noise does not carry the theme.

questions.stem: Which two details best show what prompts Mateo to change and how he changes? Choose two.
options: He searches the cabinets for his grandfather's watch
He takes the job because his mother arranged it
He watches the second hand of the repaired watch sweep around
He tells his uncle about the watch he broke
He writes the ticket for the nurse's watch
questions.explanation: Watching the repaired watch tick is what prompts him to speak, and admitting the broken watch after six years of silence is the change itself. Searching the cabinets is what he did as a nine-year-old to hide the truth, not a change.

questions.stem: Based on paragraphs 5 and 6, the reader can infer that Mateo
options: believes his grandfather broke the watch
still feels guilty about the broken watch
has forgotten exactly what happened to the watch
plans to sell the watch when he is older
questions.explanation: He has kept the watch hidden for years and still takes the sock out at night without unwrapping it, which shows lasting guilt. He clearly remembers exactly what happened.

questions.stem:
Read paragraphs 12 and 13. Select the sentence that best supports the idea that Tio Ramon accepts Mateo's confession without judging him.

{{His uncle did not ask how it had broken.}} {{He only took a fresh white cloth from the drawer and spread it on the bench between them.}} {{"Bring it next Saturday," he said.}} {{"You can do the unscrewing."}}
questions.explanation: By not asking how the watch broke, Tio Ramon makes clear that blame is not the point. Spreading the cloth and inviting Mateo back show he is ready to help, but it is the missing question that shows he is not judging.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best summary of the story?
options: Mateo works at his uncle's shop, where forty clocks tick on the walls, and a nurse arrives with a pocket watch she dropped
A customer's broken watch reminds Mateo of a watch he broke and hid, and after seeing his uncle fix it, he admits his secret
Tio Ramon repairs a nurse's watch in a single day after losing a spring, then offers Mateo a raise for his Saturday work
Mateo breaks his grandfather's watch, searches the house for it, and later learns to repair clocks in his uncle's shop
questions.explanation: A summary keeps the main events in order: the nurse's watch, Mateo's memory, the repair and his confession. The shop and the nurse are only the opening, and Mateo never learns to repair clocks in the story; he is only invited to try.

questions.stem: In paragraph 8, the comparison of Tio Ramon to a surgeon who lays out instruments mainly suggests that he is
options: tired and bored
precise and careful
nervous and rushed
proud and a little boastful
questions.explanation: A surgeon lays out tools in exact rows before careful work, and the next sentences say Tio Ramon worked without hurrying. Nothing in the paragraph suggests he is nervous or rushed.

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, the author uses the short sentence "It spun." mainly to
options: show Mateo's pride in his trick
explain how a pocket watch is built
suggest that the watch was not damaged
make the accident feel sudden
questions.explanation: The two-word sentence comes right before the watch skates off the table, so its abruptness makes the accident feel quick and sudden. The next sentences show the watch was damaged.

questions.stem:
Read paragraph 1. Select the sentence that states the author's claim.

{{Step outside in the center of almost any Texas city after sunset and look up.}} {{If you can count more than a handful of stars, you are lucky.}} {{The sky above most of our towns glows a dull orange, lit not by the moon but by millions of bulbs pointed in the wrong direction.}} {{Our cities should require outdoor lights to be shielded and aimed downward, and they should turn off lights that no one needs.}}
questions.explanation: The last sentence of paragraph 1 states the position the essay argues for: shield lights, aim them down and turn off unneeded ones. The orange sky is evidence of the problem, not the claim.

questions.stem: How does the author respond to the counterargument in paragraph 4?
options: By arguing that streetlights have never made any street safer
By granting that safety matters, then showing shielded lights help
By claiming that most people do not walk at night
By admitting that dark skies matter less than safety
questions.explanation: The author concedes that safety matters, then rebuts the objection by explaining that a downward fixture puts more light on the sidewalk. The author never says streetlights are useless.

questions.stem: The story about the volunteer and the shoebox of warblers in paragraph 3 is mainly an appeal to the reader's
options: emotions
sense of humor
respect for experts
wish to save money
questions.explanation: A shoebox filled with dead songbirds, ending with "None of them had to die," is meant to make readers feel sorrow. The money argument comes in paragraph 2.

questions.stem: Which organizational pattern does the author mainly use in paragraph 5?
options: Solution, listing steps that would fix the problem
Comparison, weighing Texas against other states
Chronological order, tracing the history of lighting
Cause and effect, showing why birds migrate
questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 lists changes cities and homeowners can make, so it presents solutions to the problem described earlier. It does not trace history or compare states.

questions.stem: Which detail best shows that the author is writing mainly for Texas residents?
options: Texas lies under one of the great routes of migrating birds
Glare from an unshielded bulb can make it much harder to see
A lit doorway helps a family find their way home
People lived under a sky full of stars for most of history
questions.explanation: Pointing out that Texas lies under a migration route tells readers in Texas why the problem is theirs. The other details would apply to readers anywhere.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of paragraph 2?
options: Light that is aimed badly wastes money
Businesses should close their parking lots
Streetlights cost cities too much to repair
Neighbors often complain about bright bulbs
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 argues that light shining sideways or up lights nothing useful, so part of the power bill buys nothing. Repair costs are never mentioned.

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, the author mentions squinting into a floodlight most likely to suggest that
options: most people prefer bright light at night
the author has trouble seeing at night
floodlights are needed to light sidewalks
too much glare can make people less safe
questions.explanation: The author is answering the safety objection, and the floodlight example shows that glare can make it harder to see, so more light is not always safer.

questions.stem: In paragraph 1, the author describes the sky as glowing "a dull orange." The word dull suggests that the glow is
options: rare and quite surprising
bright and exciting
unpleasant and lifeless
warm and comforting
questions.explanation: Dull carries a negative connotation of something flat and lifeless, which fits the author's view that lit skies have lost their stars.

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, the author's statement "No one is proposing that" responds to
options: a red herring about migrating birds
an overstatement about the cost of electricity
an understatement about how beautiful the stars are
a straw man that distorts the author's view
questions.explanation: Critics are said to claim the author wants to turn off every streetlight, an exaggerated version of the real proposal, which is a straw man. The author answers it by restating the actual position.

questions.stem: The author's main purpose in paragraph 6 is to
options: introduce a new reason to reduce outdoor lighting
explain how the Milky Way can be seen with a telescope
end with a hopeful picture of what the rules could do
admit that a dark sky may not be possible in big cities
questions.explanation: The conclusion looks ahead to children seeing the Milky Way from their yards, a hopeful image that sums up the benefit of the rules. It adds no new reason.

questions.stem: In "Learning the River," why does the poet set the last two lines apart, each beginning with "Now I am the one"?
options: To describe the speaker's first time in the water
To show that the speaker is still afraid of the deep river
To stress that the speaker now has the brother's role
To suggest that the brother has moved far away
questions.explanation: The repeated opening makes the final lines echo each other and mark the shift: the speaker now stands in the river and waits, as the brother once did. Nothing says the speaker is still afraid.

questions.stem: Which line from "Learning the River" marks the turning point of the poem?
options: and held out both his hands.
every reason not to:
as if it had somewhere better to be.
When I finally stepped in, the water
questions.explanation: Until that line the speaker stands on the bank listing reasons not to go in; stepping in is the moment the poem turns from fear toward the closing lines.

questions.stem: In "Learning the River," the simile "like a fist, / then loosened, then let me go" mainly shows that the speaker's fear
options: was strong at first but quickly eased
grew stronger the longer the speaker stayed
came from the cold more than the current
disappeared before the speaker stepped in
questions.explanation: A fist closing and then loosening shows a tight grip of fear that relaxes once the speaker is in. The fear does not vanish before the speaker steps in.

questions.stem: In paragraph 6 of "The Dock," the narrator calls the father's choice "the most embarrassing and the most comforting thing he ever did." This contrast mainly shows that the narrator
options: did not notice him until much later
wished he had stayed on the beach
is still angry that the father followed
has mixed feelings about his care
questions.explanation: Pairing embarrassing with comforting shows two feelings at once: the narrator is a little embarrassed to be followed and also glad the father was there. Nothing suggests lasting anger.

questions.stem: Why does the author of "The Dock" include the father's story about the stock tank in paragraph 2?
options: To reveal that the father knows fear from experience
To explain why the family once moved away from West Texas
To show that the grandfather was a strict parent
To warn readers about swimming in stock tanks
questions.explanation: The father shares his own near-drowning when the narrator panics, showing he knows the fear the narrator feels. Paragraph 4 confirms it: "I still don't like deep water."

questions.stem: In paragraph 5 of "The Dock," the phrase "tête-à-tête" means
options: a meal shared at the end of a long day
a private talk between two people
a quiet walk along the shore
a race between two swimmers
questions.explanation: Tete-a-tete, borrowed from French, means a private talk between two people, and the paragraph says the narrator asked the father questions until the mosquitoes came.

questions.stem: What can the reader infer from paragraph 5 of "The Dock"?
options: The narrator's father wanted to talk only about swimming
The narrator decided to stop the swimming lessons for the summer
The father's fear made the narrator see him in a new way
The mosquitoes kept the narrator from sleeping that night
questions.explanation: The narrator says it had never occurred to them that the father could be afraid, then asks questions never thought of before, so the narrator sees him in a new way.

questions.stem: In "Learning the River," what is the most important idea about the brother?
options: He argues with the speaker about the cold
He helps the speaker by waiting patiently
He leaves the speaker alone on the bank
He teaches the speaker how to catch fish
questions.explanation: The poem says the brother "did not argue. He only waited," and the speaker later takes up that same role. He does not argue at all.

questions.stem: How are the brother in "Learning the River" and the father in "The Dock" alike?
options: Both stay in the water close to the learner
Both shout instructions from out of the water
Both give up when the child is afraid
Both admit that they cannot swim very well
questions.explanation: The brother stands in the river with his hands out, and the father wades out and stays close enough to touch. The father says he does not believe in shouting from the shore.

questions.stem: Which two statements describe a difference between the two selections? Choose two.
options: Only "Learning the River" ends with the learner taking the helper's place
Only "Learning the River" takes place in summer
Only "The Dock" describes a child who is afraid of water
Only "The Dock" is told by the person being taught
Only "The Dock" shows the helper admitting a fear
questions.explanation: The father in "The Dock" admits he is afraid of deep water, while the brother in the poem shows no fear; and the poem ends with the speaker now standing in the river and waiting. Both selections describe a frightened child, and both are told by the person being taught.

questions.stem: Daniel wants to replace sentence 2 with a sentence that better introduces the main idea of his essay. Which sentence should he use?
options: These bats are also among the best friends of Texas farmers.
Watching bats is a fun thing to do on a summer night.
Many people have never seen a bat up close.
Bats belong to the only group of mammals that can truly fly.
questions.explanation: The essay goes on to explain how bats eat crop pests and need protection, so a sentence about their value to farmers introduces that idea. Sentence 2 says only that bats are interesting.

questions.stem: Which sentence should be deleted because it does not support the main idea of the second paragraph (sentences 6 through 10)?
options: Sentence 7
Sentence 8
Sentence 9
Sentence 10
questions.explanation: The second paragraph is about bats eating insects that harm crops. Sentence 9, about people fearing bats because of movies, does not support that idea.

questions.stem:
Choose the best transition to begin sentence 10.

(10) [[1]] farmers who have bats nearby may need to spray fewer chemicals on their fields.
questions.explanation: Sentence 10 states a result of bats eating crop pests, so "As a result" shows the cause-and-effect link. "However" would signal a contrast that is not there.

questions.stem: What is the most effective way to combine sentences 3 and 4?
options: Some of the largest bat colonies in the world live in the state, one of these colonies spends its summers in Bracken Cave.
Some of the largest bat colonies in the world live in the state, and one of these colonies, it spends its summers in Bracken Cave.
Some of the world's largest bat colonies live in the state, including one that summers in Bracken Cave near San Antonio.
Some of the largest bat colonies live in the state, so one of these colonies spends summers in a cave called Bracken Cave.
questions.explanation: Turning sentence 4 into an "including" phrase joins the ideas smoothly and correctly. Joining two sentences with only a comma creates a comma splice, and "so" wrongly suggests one fact causes the other.

questions.stem:
Daniel wants to replace the vague word "stuff" in sentence 14. Choose the best revision.

(14) Bats help us, and we should [[1]].
blanks: be nice and try to do things for them
protect the places where they live
help out the bats with stuff
questions.explanation: "Protect the places where they live" is precise and connects to sentences 12 and 13 about roosts. The other choices keep vague words like stuff and things.

questions.stem: Daniel wants to revise sentence 11 so that it introduces the final paragraph more clearly. Which revision is best?
options: Bats, which fly at night, face many serious threats.
Bats do so much for us, yet they face serious threats.
Serious threats, bats face them.
Bats face threats that are serious ones.
questions.explanation: Linking the threats to what bats do for us connects the last paragraph to the one before it and reads clearly. The other revisions are wordy or awkward and add no connection.

questions.stem: Daniela wants to add a sentence after sentence 3 to support her point that students have no safe place to cross. Which sentence is best?
options: The city has many other roads that need repair.
Our school was built more than forty years ago.
Many other students ride the bus or get a ride from their parents.
Walking to the light adds about twenty minutes to the trip.
questions.explanation: Showing how long the walk to the light takes explains why students do not use it, which supports her point. The other sentences do not develop the idea.

questions.stem: Daniela wants to begin the second paragraph with a topic sentence. Which sentence should she add before sentence 4?
options: Without a crosswalk, students face danger every morning.
Our school has a large and active student council.
Many cities across Texas have added new crosswalks lately.
Some students live too far from school to walk.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph describes students darting across traffic, speeding drivers and a near miss, so a topic sentence about the danger introduces it. The student council does not appear until sentence 10.

questions.stem:
Choose the revision that makes sentence 9 parallel.

(9) A crosswalk with flashing lights would remind drivers to slow down, make students visible, and [[1]] a safe route to school.
questions.explanation: The series needs three matching verb phrases: remind, make and give. "It would give" and "giving" break the pattern.

questions.stem: What is the best way to revise sentence 8?
options: Running across the road, her backpack fell open and spilled into the lane.
As she ran across the road, her backpack fell open and spilled into the lane.
Her backpack, running across the road, fell open and spilled into the lane.
Running across the road, the lane was where her backpack fell open and spilled.
questions.explanation: "Running across the road" describes the girl, but the sentence makes it modify the backpack. Turning the phrase into a clause with "she" fixes the dangling modifier.

questions.stem:
Daniela wants sentence 11 to use language that fits a formal letter to a council member. Choose the best revision.

(11) [[1]]
blanks: Seriously, this is super important, so you need to fix it right now.
I respectfully ask the council to approve a crosswalk this year.
This thing is a really big deal, so please do something about it soon.
Hopefully you guys will do something about this crosswalk problem soon.
questions.explanation: A letter to an elected official calls for a respectful, specific request. The other choices are informal or vague ("this thing," "you guys").

questions.stem: What is the correct way to write sentence 3?
options: I had to wake up at five o'clock, so I was usually still half asleep when we loaded the truck.
I had to wake up at five o'clock, I was usually still half asleep, when we loaded the truck.
I had to wake up at five o'clock I was usually still half asleep when we loaded the truck.
I had to wake up at five o'clock, and, I was usually still half asleep when we loaded the truck.
questions.explanation: Sentence 3 is a comma splice: two complete sentences joined by only a comma. Adding the conjunction "so" after the comma fixes it; removing the comma creates a run-on.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct pronoun for sentence 5.

(5) By then, farmers who sell there had to set up [[1]] own tables and shade tents.
questions.explanation: The antecedent, farmers, is plural, so the pronoun must be the plural "their." "His" and "its" are singular.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct verb for sentence 9.

(9) By the end of June, though, I knew the regular customers by name, and some of them [[1]] for me when they arrived.
questions.explanation: The essay is told in the past tense, and "knew" and "arrived" are past, so "asked" keeps the tense consistent.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct way to write the word that belongs in sentence 7.

(7) She also taught me a few words of [[1]] so that I could greet the customers who stopped by her booth.
questions.explanation: Names of languages are proper nouns and are capitalized: Spanish.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct spelling for sentence 11.

(11) I also learned that I could [[1]] a compliment without turning red.
questions.explanation: Receive follows the rule "i before e except after c": r-e-c-e-i-v-e.

questions.stem: What is the best way to correct sentences 7 and 8?
options: At the same time; workers pumped sand under the city to raise the ground behind the wall.
At the same time workers. Pumped sand under the city to raise the ground behind the wall.
At the same time, and workers pumped sand under the city to raise the ground behind the wall.
At the same time, workers pumped sand under the city to raise the ground behind the wall.
questions.explanation: "At the same time" is a fragment on its own. Attaching it to sentence 8 as an introductory phrase followed by a comma makes one complete sentence.

questions.stem: What is the correct way to write sentence 9?
options: The project was enormous: homes, churches, and even water pipes had to be lifted while the sand was poured beneath them.
The project was enormous; and homes, churches, and even water pipes had to be lifted while the sand was poured beneath them.
The project was enormous homes, churches, and even water pipes, had to be lifted while the sand was poured beneath them.
The project was enormous, homes, churches, and even water pipes had to be lifted while the sand was poured beneath them.
questions.explanation: Sentence 9 runs two sentences together. A colon fits because the second clause explains why the project was enormous; a comma alone would create a comma splice.

questions.stem: Which revision of sentence 10 uses the active voice correctly?
options: Thousands of workers built the wall over many years.
The wall had been built by thousands of workers over many years.
Over many years, the wall was being built by thousands of workers.
The wall, over many years, was built by thousands of workers.
questions.explanation: In the active voice the subject does the action: workers built the wall. The other revisions keep the passive "was built by" or "had been built by."

questions.stem:
Choose the correct way to write the word that belongs in sentence 13.

(13) Most visitors do not realize that they are standing on one of the [[1]] great engineering projects.
questions.explanation: The great projects belong to one country, so the singular possessive needs an apostrophe before the s: country's.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct punctuation for sentence 12.

(12) Today, the seawall is a popular place [[1]] and watch the waves.
questions.explanation: A colon cannot separate a verb or "to" from the words that complete it, so no colon belongs after "to." Items in a series are separated by commas: walk, ride bikes, and watch.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of Noelle's lines spoken "to the audience" about Grace?
options: To share a belief about Grace that soon proves wrong
To show that Noelle has already decided to quit the drama club
To explain to Mr. Park why Noelle wants the lead role
To let Grace overhear what Noelle truly thinks about the play
questions.explanation: This aside tells the audience that Grace never had to wait. A few lines later Grace reveals she was not cast as a freshman, so the aside sets up a belief the play overturns. Grace cannot hear an aside.

questions.stem: Why does the playwright include the stage direction that Mr. Park "does not see the girls at first"?
options: So Noelle can decide to quit without anyone seeing her
So the audience overhears a hint of trouble before Mr. Park speaks to Noelle
So the audience knows that Mr. Park is angry with Noelle
So Grace has time to leave before Mr. Park notices her
questions.explanation: Because he does not notice the girls, Mr. Park takes his phone call openly ("We'll manage"), which hints that something has changed before he turns to Noelle. Nothing shows anger, and Grace stays on stage.

questions.stem: Why does Grace tell Noelle that she was not cast as a freshman?
options: To prove that she has always been a better actor than Noelle
To show Noelle that waiting is not the same as failing
To convince Noelle to start painting sets
To explain why she stopped acting after that year
questions.explanation: Grace shares a secret she never told anyone so that Noelle, who feels the understudy role is nothing, sees that a setback is not the end. Grace was the lead in later plays, so she did not stop acting.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses a theme of the play?
options: Patience through disappointment can bring new chances
Older siblings always understand more than younger ones
Telling the truth to family members is always difficult
Hard work matters less than luck in the theater
questions.explanation: Noelle learns every line as the understudy and is about to quit, and then the chance to play the lead arrives. The play does not suggest that siblings always understand more.

questions.stem: How does the revelation at the end, "I had the email written," affect the plot?
options: It explains why Priya's family is moving to Houston
It suggests that Grace wrote the email for Noelle
It shows how close Noelle came to losing her chance
It reveals that Mr. Park had read Noelle's email
questions.explanation: Noelle admits she had written an email to quit that very night, which makes Mr. Park's offer feel like a narrow escape. Nothing shows that Mr. Park saw the email.

questions.stem: Based on Grace's final line, "Mom said that, too," the reader can infer that
options: their mother wanted Noelle to quit the play
Grace came because she knew Noelle was upset
Grace had planned to quit the drama club as well
Grace told their mother about the cast list first
questions.explanation: Their mother had told Grace that Noelle meant to quit, which explains why Grace came with two cups of lemonade. Nothing suggests their mother wanted Noelle to quit.

questions.stem: Why does Mr. Park ask Noelle how well she knows the second act?
options: He plans to cut the second act from the play
Noelle asked to be considered for a bigger part
He wants to test whether she has studied her lines
The lead actor will not be there for opening night
questions.explanation: Mr. Park explains that Priya's family is moving and she will miss opening night, so he wants Noelle to run the act.

questions.stem: Which of these is the best summary of the play?
options: Noelle and Grace drink lemonade on the stage of a high school auditorium while they talk about the cast list that was posted that afternoon
Mr. Park takes a phone call from Priya, who is moving to Houston, and decides to cancel opening night of the play until a new lead is found
Upset to be an understudy, Noelle learns that Grace once faced a setback, and then Mr. Park offers Noelle the chance to play the lead
Grace tells Noelle that she painted sets as a freshman, and the sisters decide that Noelle should join the stage crew for the spring play
questions.explanation: A summary gives the main events in order: Noelle's disappointment, Grace's story and Mr. Park's offer. The lemonade is a detail, and no one cancels opening night.

questions.stem: In the play, the word understudy means an actor who
options: learns a role to replace the lead if needed
plays several small roles in one single play
paints the sets and gathers the props
directs the other actors during rehearsals
questions.explanation: Noelle explains that she learns every line and goes to every rehearsal but watches Priya perform, which describes an actor ready to step in for the lead.

questions.stem: How do the stage directions at the start of the play help create its mood?
options: A bright spotlight on Noelle makes the whole scene feel tense and dramatic
A crowded auditorium makes the scene feel busy and exciting
A single work light on an empty stage makes the scene feel lonely
A noisy cafeteria makes the scene feel playful and relaxed
questions.explanation: The directions describe a single work light on an empty stage in late afternoon, which sets a quiet, lonely mood as Noelle sits alone.

questions.stem: Which sentence from paragraph 1 states the thesis of the article?
options: Saving the ocelot depends on two things: protecting the brush it needs and helping it travel safely between the patches that are left.
Today only a small number are known to breed in the United States, all in the southern tip of the state, and the species is listed as endangered.
Ocelots once ranged across much of South and Central Texas.
The ocelot is about twice the size of a house cat, with a coat of black spots and stripes on gold fur.
questions.explanation: The sentence about protecting brush and safe travel names the two ideas the article develops in its later sections. The other sentences give background facts about the cat.

questions.stem: How is the section "Danger on the Road" (paragraphs 3 and 4) mainly organized?
options: Two kinds of wild cats are compared
Events are given in the order they happened
A problem is described and then a solution
An idea is defined and then explained by examples
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 explains that cars kill many ocelots, and paragraph 4 describes the wildlife crossings built to reduce those deaths, a problem-and-solution pattern.

questions.stem: Which two details from the article best support the idea that wildlife crossings can help ocelots? Choose two.
options: Ocelots hunt at night and hide in thick brush during the day.
Fences guide animals toward the tunnels under the highways.
Cameras in the tunnels have recorded ocelots using them.
Most land in Texas is privately owned.
Brush planted today will take years to grow thick.
questions.explanation: Camera records show ocelots really use the tunnels, and the fences steer animals to them instead of onto the road. The other details are about brush or ownership, not crossings.

questions.stem: How does paragraph 5 build on the ideas in paragraph 4?
options: It describes how ocelots were first found in Texas
It explains that crossings need habitat to connect
It compares ocelots with other animals in the tunnels
It argues that crossings are too costly to build
questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 opens with "Crossings cannot help if there is nowhere for the cats to go," linking the tunnels in paragraph 4 to the need for restored brush. Cost is never discussed.

questions.stem: Why is paragraph 6 an effective conclusion to the article?
options: It tells readers exactly how many ocelots are left
It admits the work is slow but links each step to the thesis
It shifts the topic from ocelots to bobcats and other wild cats
It adds a new fact about the size of the ocelot
questions.explanation: The conclusion acknowledges that restored brush takes years to grow, then connects each crossing and acre back to the thesis about helping young ocelots travel. It gives no new count or topic.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, why must young ocelots cross open land?
options: They leave home to find territory of their own
They follow their mothers to new hunting areas at night
They are driven away by bobcats in the brush
They hunt for food in open farm fields
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says young ocelots that leave home to find their own territory must cross open land to reach another patch. Ocelots avoid open ground when they can.

questions.stem: What can the reader infer about the private landowners described in paragraph 5?
options: They are paid to leave brush on their land
Their choices can affect whether ocelots survive
They plan to sell their ranches to refuges
They have seen more ocelots than biologists have
questions.explanation: Because most land in Texas is private, a ranch that keeps a strip of brush can link two patches, so landowners' choices matter to the cats. Nothing says they are paid.

questions.stem: In paragraph 1, the word dense most likely means
options: tall and widely spaced
green and full of flowers
dry, brittle and easily broken
thick and crowded together
questions.explanation: The article says ocelots hide in dense thorny shrubs and need cover, which points to brush that is thick and crowded together.

questions.stem: How do the headings help the reader?
options: They show the dates when each event happened
They show the problem or step each part covers
They tell the reader which of the facts are really opinions
They list the sources the author used
questions.explanation: "Losing Ground," "Danger on the Road" and "Room to Grow" each name the problem or solution the section explains, so readers can follow the article's structure.

questions.stem: In paragraph 6, the phrase "the place its ancestors once ruled" mainly adds
options: a fact about how ocelots raise their young
a hint that ocelots will soon disappear
a sense of what the ocelot has lost
a warning that ocelots are dangerous
questions.explanation: Describing the land as a place the ocelot's ancestors "once ruled" stresses how much of its range the cat has lost. The paragraph is hopeful, not a prediction that ocelots will vanish.

questions.stem: In "Monarchs, October," how does the second line help the reader picture the migration?
options: Its short length shows that only a few butterflies came
Its rhyme with the first line makes the scene sound playful
Its growing numbers show the crowd of butterflies swelling
Its question invites the reader to count the butterflies
questions.explanation: "A few, then dozens, then more than I can count" builds from small to large, so the line itself grows the way the crowd of butterflies does. The line does not rhyme or ask a question.

questions.stem: What is the effect of the repeated words "None of them" in lines 5 and 6 of the poem?
options: They suggest that the speaker is disappointed in the monarchs
They explain why the butterflies stop to rest in the parking lot
They show that the butterflies are lost and flying around in circles
They stress how remarkable it is that the monarchs know the way
questions.explanation: The repetition points out that no butterfly has made the trip before or will make it twice, which makes the next lines, "And still they know the way," more striking.

questions.stem: In the poem, the simile comparing the butterflies to "a song" that "knows where it ends" suggests that their journey is
options: loud and hard to follow
planned out by the speaker
short and quickly forgotten
natural and certain
questions.explanation: A song moves naturally toward its ending, so the comparison shows the monarchs following their route with a certainty they were born with.

questions.stem: What do the last two lines of the poem reveal about the speaker?
options: The speaker is late and annoyed by the butterflies
The speaker has lost the car keys in the parking lot
The speaker plans to follow the monarchs south
The monarchs pull the speaker out of an ordinary day
questions.explanation: The speaker stands with keys in hand and forgets, for a minute, where they were going, which shows the butterflies have interrupted an ordinary errand with wonder.

questions.stem: What is the author's main purpose in paragraph 4 of "A Highway for Butterflies"?
options: To explain how far monarchs fly in a single day
To urge readers to plant small gardens for monarchs
To warn readers not to touch monarch caterpillars
To describe the fir trees where monarchs spend winter
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 begins "Anyone can help" and describes pots of milkweed and schoolyard patches, so it urges readers to act.

questions.stem: In paragraph 3 of "A Highway for Butterflies," the word habitat means
options: a law that protects wildlife
a road or path built for traveling animals
a kind of plant that grows wild along roads
a place that meets a living thing's needs
questions.explanation: The roadside strips of milkweed and flowers give monarchs food and places to breed, which is what habitat means: a place that meets a living thing's needs.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2 of "A Highway for Butterflies," why is milkweed important to monarchs?
options: It gives adults nectar for their long flight
It marks the route to Mexico for the adults
It is the only food their caterpillars eat
It protects the butterflies from cold weather
questions.explanation: The article says caterpillars eat only milkweed, so females must find it to lay eggs. Adults drink nectar from other flowers for energy.

questions.stem: Based on paragraph 3 of "A Highway for Butterflies," highway workers most likely changed their mowing because
options: the highway became too crowded to mow safely
frequent mowing cut flowers before they bloomed
monarchs were damaging the mowing equipment
the states ran out of money to pay for mowing
questions.explanation: The paragraph says workers changed when and how often they mow "so that flowers have time to bloom," which implies earlier mowing cut flowers down too soon.

questions.stem: Which idea appears in both selections?
options: People can plant gardens to help the monarchs
Monarchs spend the winter on fir trees in Mexico
No single monarch makes the whole round trip
Monarch caterpillars eat only milkweed plants
questions.explanation: The poem says none will make the trip twice, and the article says no single butterfly completes the whole cycle. The fir trees, milkweed and gardens appear only in the article.

questions.stem: How is the poem's view of the migration different from the article's?
options: The poem gives facts, while the article tells a personal story
The poem argues for change, while the article describes a single afternoon
The poem focuses on caterpillars, while the article focuses on adults
The poem expresses wonder, while the article explains what monarchs need
questions.explanation: The poem describes one speaker's amazement at the butterflies, while the article explains the route, the plants monarchs depend on and how people can help.

questions.stem: Which sentence should be deleted because it does not support the main idea of the second paragraph (sentences 4 through 8)?
options: Sentence 5
Sentence 6
Sentence 7
Sentence 8
questions.explanation: The second paragraph lists reasons a cooking class helps students. Sentence 7, about when the writer's brother learned to cook, gives no reason and does not support that idea.

questions.stem:
Choose the best transition to begin sentence 10.

(10) [[1]] a cooking class could take the place of one semester of an elective.
questions.explanation: Sentence 9 gives an objection and sentence 10 answers it, so "However" signals the contrast. "As a result" would wrongly make sentence 10 follow from the objection.

questions.stem: Which sentence could best be added after sentence 11 to strengthen the writer's response to the counterargument?
options: Many students already take an elective only to fill an empty period in their schedule.
Cooking shows have become very popular on television in recent years.
Some students prefer art or music to cooking.
The cafeteria serves lunch to hundreds of students every single day.
questions.explanation: The objection is that there is no room for a new required class. Pointing out that many students take an elective only to fill an empty period shows the schedule does have room for the class. The other sentences do not answer the objection.

questions.stem: What is the best way to revise sentence 8 to make the transition clearer?
options: Also, a cooking class, it teaches math and science, such as measuring ingredients and understanding how heat changes food.
Also a cooking class teaches math, also science, such as measuring ingredients and understanding how heat changes food.
