A cooking class also teaches math and science, such as measuring ingredients and understanding how heat changes food.
In conclusion, a cooking class teaches math and science, such as measuring ingredients and understanding how heat changes food.
questions.explanation: Placing "also" after the subject reads smoothly and still signals another reason. "In conclusion" is wrong because the paragraph does not end the essay, and repeating "also" is awkward.

questions.stem:
The writer wants a stronger final sentence. Choose the best revision of sentence 13.

(13) [[1]]
blanks: No student should graduate without knowing how to cook a meal.
Cooking is a thing that is good, and that is my opinion on it.
So that is why cooking is good and why we should all do cooking.
Learning to cook is good and our school should do it.
questions.explanation: The revision restates the claim with a precise, memorable image. The other choices are vague ("good," "a thing") or repeat words without adding meaning.

questions.stem: What is the most effective way to combine sentences 10 and 11?
options: A cooking class could take the place of one semester of an elective, and also there would be time.
A cooking class could take the place of one semester of an elective, students would still have time.
Because students would still have time for other subjects, a cooking class could take an elective's place.
A cooking class could replace one semester of an elective, leaving time for other subjects.
questions.explanation: The phrase "leaving time for other subjects" joins the ideas clearly and correctly. Joining with only a comma makes a comma splice, and "because" reverses the logic.

questions.stem:
The writer wants to replace sentence 8 with a sentence that better develops the idea of the paragraph. Choose the best revision.

(8) [[1]]
blanks: It was a really pretty and nice yellow color.
Every stitch was a costly gift.
I liked the dress a lot when I saw it.
questions.explanation: The paragraph is about the work and money that went into the dress, so a sentence about each stitch as a costly gift develops that idea. "The dress was very nice" adds nothing.

questions.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 14 to avoid repeating sentence 3. Which revision is best?
options: The dress was old, and that is what I thought about it.
I used to think the dress was only old and nothing else.
I thought the dress was just old, as I said before in my essay.
For years, I walked past that dress without a second look.
questions.explanation: Sentence 3 already says the writer thought it was "just an old dress." The revision keeps the idea of overlooking the dress without repeating the wording, which sets up the final sentence.

questions.stem: What is the most effective way to combine sentences 12 and 13?
options: She was tired but kept working.
Being tired, working was kept up anyway.
She was tired, she kept working anyway.
She was tired and working anyway kept.
questions.explanation: The conjunction "but" joins two complete sentences and shows the contrast between being tired and working. Joining them with only a comma makes a comma splice.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that most precisely describes the great-grandmother in sentence 11.

(11) When I looked in the mirror, I thought about my great-grandmother [[1]] over her sewing machine.
questions.explanation: "Hunched" is precise and shows the tiring work. "Being" and "there" are vague, and "sitting down" does not describe her posture.

questions.stem: What is the best way to revise sentence 7 so the phrase "in a whole year" is placed clearly?
options: The fabric had cost more than the family usually spent on clothes in a whole year.
The fabric had cost more than in a whole year the family usually spent on clothes.
In a whole year, the fabric had cost more than the family usually spent on clothes.
The fabric, in a whole year, had cost more than the family usually spent on clothes.
questions.explanation: "In a whole year" belongs with what the family usually spent on clothes. Placed near "the fabric" or "had cost," it makes the fabric seem to cost that much every year.

questions.stem: What is the best way to correct sentences 5 and 6?
options: Cowboys drove herds of thousands of cattle north to railroad towns in Kansas; such as Abilene.
Cowboys drove herds of thousands of cattle north. To railroad towns in Kansas, such as Abilene.
Cowboys drove herds of thousands of cattle north to railroad towns in Kansas. Such as, Abilene.
Cowboys drove herds of thousands of cattle north to railroad towns in Kansas, such as Abilene.
questions.explanation: "Such as Abilene" is a fragment. Joining it to sentence 5 with a comma makes one complete sentence; a semicolon must join two complete sentences.

questions.stem: Which revision of sentence 9 is written correctly?
options: The cowboys crossed rivers, faced storms, and survived stampedes.
The cowboys crossed rivers, the weather could be dangerous, and stampedes.
The cowboys crossed rivers, dangerous weather, and there were stampedes.
The cowboys crossed rivers and the weather, and stampedes were dangerous.
questions.explanation: The sentence needs a parallel series of verb phrases with one subject: crossed, faced and survived. The original mixes a clause, another clause and a bare noun.

questions.stem:
Choose the verb that keeps the tense consistent in sentence 10.

(10) Each night, the cowboys [[1]] turns watching the herd.
questions.explanation: The rest of the essay tells about the cattle drives in the past tense, so the past tense "took" keeps the verbs consistent. "Take" shifts the essay into the present.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct way to write the word that belongs in sentence 11.

(11) By the end of the 1880s, railroads had reached [[1]], and the long drives came to an end.
questions.explanation: Names of states are proper nouns and are capitalized: Texas.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct way to write the words that belong in sentence 12.

(12) In less than twenty years, though, the trail had become a lasting part of the history of [[1]].
questions.explanation: "West" is capitalized when it names a region, as in the American West, and "American" is always capitalized. "The" is lowercase in the middle of a sentence.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct way to write sentence 3.

(3) [[1]]
blanks: Our club meets after school we need a quiet place to play.
Our club meets after school, and, we need a quiet place to play.
Our club meets after school, we need a quiet place to play.
Since our club meets after school, we need a quiet place to play.
questions.explanation: The original joins two sentences with only a comma. Making the first part a dependent clause with "since" fixes the comma splice; removing the comma makes a run-on.

questions.stem:
Choose the verb that keeps the tense consistent in sentence 6.

(6) Last week, our members [[1]] to stop a game three times because of the noise.
questions.explanation: "Last week" shows the event is in the past, so the past tense "had" is correct.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct punctuation for sentence 7.

(7) The study room, which has a large table and a door that [[1]] would be ideal.
questions.explanation: "Which has a large table and a door that closes" is a nonessential clause, so it is set off by a pair of commas. The original has the opening comma but not the closing one.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct punctuation for sentence 9.

(9) We would be happy to bring our own boards and [[1]] nothing in the library would be used.
questions.explanation: A comma comes before a coordinating conjunction such as "so" that joins two complete sentences. A semicolon is not used before a coordinating conjunction in a sentence like this.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct way to write the words that belong in sentence 1.

(1) My name is Tomas Reyes, and I am the president of the Chess Club at [[1]].
questions.explanation: The full name of a school is a proper noun, so each important word is capitalized: Lakeview High School.

questions.stem: How does the author develop Celeste as a foil to Ana?
options: Celeste is new and cheerful, unlike the hurt, proud Ana
Celeste blames the coach, while Ana accepts the list calmly
Celeste is Ana's oldest friend from the summer runs
Celeste trains harder than Ana and keeps detailed notes
questions.explanation: Celeste has never raced and offers to train together, while Ana, who has run for years, forces a smile and leaves. The contrast shows Ana's hurt pride. Ana is the one with the notebook.

questions.stem: Which event is the turning point of the story?
options: Celeste offers to train with Ana on the junior varsity team
Celeste admits that she hates the long hill
Ana reads the varsity list on the gym door
Ana rereads her notebook and sees why she stopped improving
questions.explanation: Reading the notebook, Ana realizes she had stopped paying attention to how she ran, and the next scene shows her ready to train differently. The list starts the conflict; it does not turn it.

questions.stem: Which theme is best supported by the story?
options: Talent always matters more than years of hard work
Coaches seldom notice the athletes who work hardest
Effort counts most with honest reflection
Competing with a friend will ruin the friendship
questions.explanation: Ana ran more than anyone but stopped noticing what her notes showed; she improves only when she reflects. The story never suggests that talent beats work.

questions.stem: How does the long hill behind the school contribute to the story?
options: It shows that the team trains only on flat roads
It is where Ana first learns she did not make varsity
It explains why Celeste walked during her first mile
It is the challenge Ana once skipped and now faces
questions.explanation: One of Ana's notebook entries says "skipped hills, too hot." Choosing to time the hill with Celeste shows she is now facing what she avoided.

questions.stem: Why does Ana walk to the parking lot "without stretching" in paragraph 4?
options: She is late for a ride waiting in the lot
She wants Celeste to follow her to the lot
She is too upset to follow her normal routine
She has decided that stretching does not help
questions.explanation: Ana has to force a smile, so skipping her stretches shows how upset she is. Nothing mentions a ride.

questions.stem: Which sentence best summarizes paragraph 5?
options: Ana's notebook shows that her times stopped improving when she stopped paying attention.
Ana's notebook lists every split she has run since she started running in sixth grade.
Ana remembers how hot it was during the summer runs before the sun came up.
Ana decides to throw away her old notebook because her slow early times now embarrass her.
questions.explanation: The paragraph shows her times leveling off in July beside notes about heavy legs and skipped hills, and ends with her realization. She keeps the notebook.

questions.stem: In paragraph 2, the word splits most likely refers to
options: injuries caused by running
groups the team is divided into
times recorded for parts of a run
races that end in a close tie
questions.explanation: Ana keeps a notebook of every split she recorded, and paragraph 5 says the pages were crowded with times, so splits are the times for parts of a run.

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, the phrase "made her mouth smile" suggests that Ana's smile is
options: joyful
shy
mocking
forced
questions.explanation: Making her mouth smile shows the smile does not come naturally; she is pushing herself to look friendly while she is upset.

questions.stem: In paragraph 1, the phrase "by 3:16 Ana knew" mainly creates a feeling of
options: how long Ana waited at the door
how quickly the disappointment hit
how late the coach posted the list
how carefully Ana planned her day
questions.explanation: The list goes up at 3:15 and she knows by 3:16, so the precise times stress how fast the disappointment arrives.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the story with Ana writing the date on a clean page?
options: To show that Ana has finished with running
To suggest that Ana is making a fresh start
To reveal that Celeste will keep Ana's notebook
To explain how Ana won a place on varsity
questions.explanation: A clean page and a new date, right after "Let's time it," signal a new beginning for Ana's training. The story never says she reaches varsity.

questions.stem: Why does the poet put the words "not yet, not yet" in italics?
options: To set the grandfather's words apart from the speaker's
To show that the grandfather shouted at the speaker
To suggest that the melon was spoiled and thrown away
To mark the title of a song the grandfather liked to whistle
questions.explanation: The italics mark the words the grandfather said as he tested a melon, separating his voice from the speaker's. Nothing suggests shouting.

questions.stem: How does the structure of the poem's last lines, each beginning with "and," affect its meaning?
options: It builds toward the moment the grandfather seems present
It lists the objects the grandfather left the speaker
It shows that the speaker is in a great hurry at the busy market
It repeats the poem's opening lines word for word
questions.explanation: Linking the final lines with "and" adds one detail after another until the closing "and there he is," when the speaker feels the grandfather's presence. The opening says he left no objects.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the theme of the poem?
options: Markets are crowded places where people feel lonely
A family should keep the objects a loved one leaves
Grandparents rarely speak about the things they value
The most lasting gifts can be habits passed down
questions.explanation: The grandfather left no watch or ring, yet his whistling and his way of testing melons live on in the speaker. Objects are exactly what he did not leave.

questions.stem: The lines "He left me the word *patience*, / though he never said it once" are an example of
options: hyperbole, exaggerating how much he said
onomatopoeia, imitating the sound of his whistle
paradox, showing he taught patience by example
alliteration, repeating sounds for rhythm
questions.explanation: It seems impossible to leave someone a word you never said. The apparent contradiction makes sense once the reader sees he taught patience by how he acted.

questions.stem: How does the speaker's tone change from the beginning of the poem to the end?
options: From curious and puzzled to bored and tired
From joyful and playful to sad and lonely
From angry and bitter to calm and forgiving
From plain and flat to tender and moved
questions.explanation: The opening flatly lists what was not left; the ending, where the aisle goes quiet "and there he is," is tender. The speaker is never angry.

questions.stem: In the poem, the word inheritance refers to
options: a lesson taught in a school class
something passed on after a death
a habit a person learns at the market
money a person earns by hard work
questions.explanation: An inheritance is what someone leaves to others after death, and the poem says what the grandfather "left me."

questions.stem: Why does the grandfather say "not yet, not yet" when he tests a melon?
options: The speaker has asked to go home early
The bread is still rising in the oven
The melon is not ripe enough to pick
The market is about to close for the day
questions.explanation: Pressing a melon with a thumb tests ripeness, and "not yet" shows it needs more time. That habit is how he teaches patience.

questions.stem: Which sentence states the author's claim?
options: The goal is understandable: phones can distract students and pull their attention away from lessons.
Teachers in many classrooms already use phones for quick quizzes and polls.
Several school districts have recently banned students from carrying phones during the school day.
Instead of locking phones away, schools should teach students when and how to use them.
questions.explanation: The last sentence of paragraph 1 states the position the essay defends. The others give background or a supporting detail.

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, how does the author treat the argument that teenagers find phones hard to resist?
options: The author agrees and decides a ban may be best
The author rejects it as a claim with no evidence behind it
The author concedes it, then uses it to support teaching
The author ignores it and moves on to a new reason
questions.explanation: The author answers "That is true" and then argues the difficulty is exactly why schools should help students practice. That is a concession followed by a rebuttal.

questions.stem: How does the author rebut the objection in paragraph 5?
options: By admitting that the objection cannot be answered
By arguing that teachers have plenty of free time
By comparing phone skills to skills schools already teach
By citing a study of how teachers spend their time each day
questions.explanation: The author points out that schools already teach email writing and online safety, so managing a phone fits on the same list. No study is cited.

questions.stem: Which kind of appeal does the author mainly use in paragraph 2?
options: Authority, quoting a well-known expert
Logic, reasoning about adult life
Humor, joking about phone pouches
Emotion, describing a frightening accident
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 reasons that adults need phone self-control at work, so school should build it. It quotes no expert and tells no frightening story.

questions.stem: The essay seems written mainly for which audience?
options: Teenagers who want new phones
Employers hiring recent graduates
Phone companies designing new apps
Parents and school leaders
questions.explanation: The essay argues about school rules and what schools should teach, the decision parents and school leaders face. Employers are mentioned only as an example.

questions.stem: Why is paragraph 6 an effective conclusion?
options: It introduces a new reason phones help learning
It summarizes what supporters of bans believe
It gives the results of a district's phone ban
It sets a short-term gain against a lifelong one
questions.explanation: The conclusion sets "quieter for a year" against help "for the rest of their lives," restating the claim memorably without new evidence.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of paragraph 3?
options: Phones can help students learn in class
Students should study with paper dictionaries
Teachers should give more quizzes and polls
Phones are the main cause of poor grades
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 lists ways phones help learning, such as photographing notes and quick quizzes, and argues a ban removes those tools.

questions.stem: Based on paragraph 2, the author most likely believes that high school should
options: keep students away from all technology
focus only on test scores and grades
prepare students for adult life
let employers decide what is taught
questions.explanation: The paragraph asks readers to "consider what students will face after graduation" and says high school should help them practice self-control for adult life.

questions.stem: In paragraph 1, the author says a total ban "treats a skill problem as a discipline problem." This sentence mainly
options: reframes the issue so a ban seems the wrong tool
suggests that teachers are much too strict with their students
proves that bans have failed in every district
admits that students cannot learn to manage phones
questions.explanation: By calling phone use a skill to learn rather than a rule to enforce, the author changes how readers see the problem and sets up the claim. It proves nothing about districts.

questions.stem: How do paragraphs 2 and 3 work together to support the claim?
options: Both describe the history of phones in schools
Paragraph 3 disproves the reason given in paragraph 2
Each gives a separate reason to teach rather than ban
Both respond to objections raised by supporters of bans
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 gives a reason about preparing for adult life and paragraph 3 a reason about phones as learning tools. The objections come in paragraphs 4 and 5.

questions.stem: In paragraph 1, the author writes "locking phones away" instead of "storing phones." The word locking suggests that a ban is
options: fair
cheap
harsh
sensible
questions.explanation: Locking something away sounds forceful and restrictive, which fits the author's view that bans control students instead of teaching them.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: A sprinkler in a front yard uses water from the aquifer.
The recharge zone lies north and west of San Antonio.
A single rain shower in the hills can fill the whole aquifer in just one day.
The Edwards Aquifer cannot be seen from the highway, but it shapes life above it every day.
questions.explanation: The article explains how the hidden aquifer supplies cities, farms and springs, and this sentence from paragraph 5 sums up that idea. The recharge zone is one detail, and the article never says one shower fills the aquifer.

questions.stem: How are paragraphs 2 and 3 organized?
options: They compare the water in the aquifer with an underground lake
They tell the history of San Antonio in time order
They explain how water enters and then how it leaves
They describe a problem and argue for one solution
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2, under "How Water Gets In," covers recharge, and paragraph 3, under "How Water Gets Out," covers wells and springs.

questions.stem: Which pattern does the author mainly use in paragraph 4?
options: Classification, sorting the animals of the springs
Definition, explaining what limestone is made of
Chronological order, listing the region's water shortages year by year
Cause and effect, from drought to falling water to new rules
questions.explanation: Drought means less water in and more pumped out, which can slow the springs; the region responds with limits. That chain is cause and effect.

questions.stem: Which detail best supports the idea that the recharge zone needs protection?
options: The springs at San Marcos are among the largest in Texas
Spills there reach the water with little filtering
The limestone rises to the surface north of San Antonio
Creeks carry water across the exposed rock after it rains
questions.explanation: Because water enters quickly in the recharge zone, a spill can reach drinking water almost unfiltered, which is why the zone must be protected.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the comparison in paragraph 1 that the aquifer is "not an underground lake"?
options: To correct a common mistake about what an aquifer is
To show that underground lakes are more common in Texas
To explain why the aquifer is shrinking each year
To argue that the aquifer should be turned into a real lake someday
questions.explanation: Many readers picture an aquifer as an underground lake, so the author corrects that and describes water-filled limestone instead.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 3, what are the two ways water leaves the aquifer?
options: Through creeks and through rain
Through lawns and through farms
Through cracks and through deep caves
Through wells and through springs
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says people pump water out through wells and it flows out naturally through springs.

questions.stem: Based on paragraphs 3 and 4, why might the blind salamander be at risk during a drought?
options: It lives only in spring-fed water that can slow to a trickle
It is often pumped out with well water
It cannot find food when farmers stop watering fields
It must travel all the way to the recharge zone to lay its eggs
questions.explanation: The salamander lives in water found nowhere else, and paragraph 4 says springs can slow to a trickle in drought, threatening their animals.

questions.stem: Which is the best summary of the article?
options: The Edwards Aquifer is an underground lake near San Antonio that rarely runs low, even in the very hottest and driest summers
The Edwards Aquifer is filled by rain in the recharge zone, feeds wells and springs, and must be managed in droughts
The Edwards Aquifer causes floods in the Hill Country when heavy rain falls on the limestone, so cities pump it out to stop them
The Edwards Aquifer is home to a blind salamander, which scientists study in the caves and channels under the Texas Hill Country
questions.explanation: A summary covers how water enters, how it leaves and why it must be balanced. The aquifer is not a lake, and the salamander is only one detail.

questions.stem: How do the headings help organize the information in the article?
options: They give the dates of the worst droughts on record
They list the cities that depend on its water
They follow the water in, out and through its management
They separate the facts in the article from the author's own opinions
questions.explanation: "How Water Gets In," "How Water Gets Out" and "Balancing the Supply" trace the water's path and how people manage it.

questions.stem: What is the author's main purpose in the article?
options: To inform readers how the aquifer works and why it matters
To describe one family's farm during a long drought
To persuade readers to move away from the Hill Country before the next drought
To entertain readers with a story about exploring caves
questions.explanation: The article explains recharge, wells, springs and drought rules, and it closes with why the aquifer matters. It tells no story.

questions.stem: In paragraph 1, the word riddled most likely means
options: full of holes
puzzling and hard to understand
worn smooth by water
hidden deep below the ground
questions.explanation: Limestone "riddled with cracks, channels and caves" is full of openings all through it, which is how water fills it. "Puzzling" is the meaning of riddle as a noun, not this use.

questions.stem: What do the stage directions about Diego's earbuds show about him at the start of the scene?
options: He is angry that he has to work late
He is waiting for an important phone call
He is listening carefully to his grandmother's stories
He is shut off from his grandmother and her concerns
questions.explanation: Diego sweeps with earbuds in and does not hear Lupe call him, which shows he is closed off from her. He takes them out as he starts to listen.

questions.stem: Why does the playwright have Diego take out his second earbud when Lupe mentions selling the building?
options: To show that he wants to leave the restaurant
To show that he did not hear her question
To show that his music has finally finished playing
To show that he now gives her his attention
questions.explanation: Removing the second earbud is a visible signal that Diego is now fully listening, the moment his attitude starts to change.

questions.stem: How does Diego change during the scene?
options: He moves from wanting to cook to wanting to sell the building
He goes from not caring about the restaurant to wanting it to last
He moves from respecting his grandmother to doubting all of her advice
He moves from working quickly to refusing to work at all
questions.explanation: At first he says nobody looks at the corner; by the end he says somebody has to keep looking at it, showing he now cares about the restaurant's future.

questions.stem: What does the corner of the floor come to stand for by the end of the scene?
options: The money Lupe could earn by selling the building
The care that has kept the restaurant going
The photographs that hang on the restaurant walls
The trouble Lupe has with her knees
questions.explanation: Lupe has looked at the corner for forty-one years, and Diego's final line turns sweeping it into a promise to keep caring for the restaurant.

questions.stem: What does Lupe's line "As if I know how to rest" reveal about her?
options: She plans to retire as soon as the building is sold
She is angry that the banker came back to the restaurant
She wants Diego to take over all of her work at once
Work has filled her life so long that rest feels strange
questions.explanation: Lupe laughs at the idea that she could rest, which shows that after forty-one years of work, resting is something she does not know how to do. Nothing shows anger at the banker.

questions.stem: What does Lupe's line "Tomorrow, come at six. I'll show you how to make the salsa" suggest?
options: She has decided to keep the place and teach Diego
She is punishing Diego for missing the corner when he swept
She plans to sell the restaurant the next morning
She wants Diego to sweep the floor again
questions.explanation: Teaching the salsa and asking him to come early show Lupe has chosen to keep going and to pass the work on to Diego. Nothing suggests punishment.

questions.stem: Why does Lupe ask Diego what he thinks about selling?
options: She needs him to sign the papers from the bank
She has already sold the building and feels guilty
She wonders whether the family will keep the business
She wants him to persuade his mother to agree with her plan
questions.explanation: His mother and her knees say sell, so asking Diego shows she wants to know whether anyone in the family will keep the restaurant going.

questions.stem: In the stage directions, Lupe sits "heavily" at the table. The word heavily suggests that she
options: is angry and impatient
is confused and lost
is weighed down
is excited and eager
questions.explanation: Sitting heavily shows weariness, and the next lines show what is weighing on her: the offer to sell.

questions.stem: In paragraph 2, the phrase carte blanche means
options: complete freedom to choose
a warning to be very careful
a written list of the day's tasks
a menu of the day's special dishes
questions.explanation: Carte blanche, from French, means full freedom to decide, and the narrator says it meant no one would tell the narrator what to do.

questions.stem: In paragraph 5, the phrase "Bon appetit" is used to
options: praise a well-made recipe
wish someone a good meal
ask for help in the kitchen
say goodbye at the end of a job
questions.explanation: Bon appetit, French for "good appetite," is a wish that someone enjoys their food, fitting for a recipe card.

questions.stem: In paragraph 3, the word frenzy most likely means
options: a quiet period between meals
a large order from one customer
a kitchen tool used for frying
wild, hurried activity
questions.explanation: The next sentence describes orders arriving faster than anyone could read them and pans clattering, which is wild, hurried activity.

questions.stem: In paragraph 3, the word deliberate means that the uncle's calm was
options: learned from a book
done on purpose
difficult to see
slow to develop
questions.explanation: The uncle explains that a calm cook has time to fix things, so his calm was intended: done on purpose.

questions.stem: In paragraph 3, the narrator says the uncle moved "almost lazily." Why does the narrator include the word almost?
options: To show the uncle only seemed lazy
To show the uncle was too tired to work quickly that day
To show the uncle was waiting for someone to help
To show the narrator thought the uncle was a poor cook
questions.explanation: Lazily alone would be a criticism; "almost" softens it, since the uncle was in fact calmly tasting and adjusting dishes.

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, the word consistent means that the narrator's work was
options: creative and full of surprises
faster than anyone else's
the same in quality each time
finished before the deadline
questions.explanation: The uncle explains that a customer expects the same dish to taste the same, so consistency means producing the same quality every time.

questions.stem: In paragraph 1, the narrator says "I suspect my mother had asked him to." The word suspect means
options: accuse of a crime
believe but not know
hope for something
remember clearly
questions.explanation: The narrator adds that neither of them ever admitted it, so the narrator believes it without proof.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 4, what did the uncle believe was the secret of the business?
options: Making dishes the same way every time
Inventing a new recipe every week
Cooking faster than other caterers
Keeping prices lower than restaurants
questions.explanation: The uncle said consistency was the whole secret, because a customer expects a dish to taste the same twice.

questions.stem: What does the recipe card in paragraph 5 suggest about the uncle's opinion of the narrator?
options: He thinks the narrator should quit cooking
He wants the narrator to sell the secret recipe for money
He trusts the narrator with something precious
He is disappointed in the narrator's work
questions.explanation: The uncle had never written the empanada recipe down for anyone, so giving it to the narrator shows trust and respect.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the details about the bowl, the tortillas and the slang in paragraph 2?
options: To explain why the uncle fired the narrator
To show how unprepared the narrator was at first
To describe the foods the catering business served
To prove that the narrator spoke Spanish well
questions.explanation: Breaking a bowl, burning tortillas and wandering between stations show the narrator was lost at first, which makes the narrator's progress by August stand out.

questions.stem: How does the final sentence of the memoir connect to the rest of the text?
options: It reveals that the narrator lost the recipe card
It suggests the narrator never cooked again
It shows the summer's lessons have stayed with the narrator
It explains why the uncle closed the catering business that fall
questions.explanation: Keeping the stained card in a wallet years later shows how much the summer and the uncle's trust still mean to the narrator.

questions.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 3 with a sentence that better introduces the topic. Which sentence is best?
options: The answer was women pilots trained in a small Texas town.
Some people at that time did not know how to fly any kind of plane.
Planes were very important to winning the war.
The answer came from people who were unexpected by many.
questions.explanation: The essay is about the women pilots trained in Sweetwater, so naming them introduces the topic. The original sentence is vague.

questions.stem: Which sentence should be deleted because it does not support the main idea of the second paragraph (sentences 4 through 8)?
options: Sentence 5
Sentence 6
Sentence 7
Sentence 8
questions.explanation: The second paragraph describes who the WASP were and what they did. Sentence 8, a fact about the size of Sweetwater, does not support that idea.

questions.stem:
Choose the best transition to begin sentence 9.

(9) [[1]] the WASP were not treated as members of the military.
questions.explanation: Sentence 9 contrasts the women's service in the previous paragraph with how they were treated, so a contrast such as "Despite their service" fits. "As a result" would suggest their service caused the poor treatment.

questions.stem:
The writer wants to replace sentence 13 with a stronger conclusion. Choose the best revision.

(13) [[1]]
blanks: They opened the sky to later women pilots.
There were a lot of them and they flew many planes.
That is the end of the whole story of the brave WASP pilots.
questions.explanation: A strong conclusion states the lasting importance of the subject. The other choices are vague or simply say the essay is over.

questions.stem: What is the most effective way to combine sentences 1 and 2?
options: During World War II, many male pilots, the United States needed pilots to fly military planes from factories to air bases, were overseas.
During World War II, the United States needed pilots to fly planes from factories to bases because many male pilots were overseas.
During World War II, the United States needed pilots to fly military planes, and also many male pilots were fighting overseas.
During World War II, the United States needed pilots to fly military planes from factories to bases, many male pilots were overseas.
questions.explanation: "Because" shows that the shortage of male pilots is the reason for the need. A comma alone creates a comma splice, and "and also" hides the cause.

questions.stem:
Choose the most precise verb for sentence 7.

(7) They [[1]] planes across the country, tested repaired aircraft, and towed targets so that gunners on the ground could practice.
questions.explanation: "Ferried" means carried from one place to another, which describes flying planes to bases exactly. "Did" and "got" are vague.

questions.stem: What is the best way to revise sentence 10 to make the relationship between ideas clearer?
options: When the program ended in 1944, their own way home, the women had to pay.
When the program ended in 1944, the women, unlike soldiers, paid their own way home.
The program ended in 1944, the women had to pay their own way home.
The program ended in 1944, and the women, they had to pay for their own long way home.
questions.explanation: Adding "unlike soldiers" shows how the women were treated differently, which is the point of the paragraph. The other revisions create a comma splice or a confusing order.

questions.stem:
The writer wants to revise sentence 11 to stress how long the women waited. Choose the best word for the blank.

(11) Congress [[1]] recognized them as veterans in 1977.
questions.explanation: "Finally" stresses how long the women waited for recognition. "Sometimes" and "really" add no meaning.

questions.stem: Which sentence in the second paragraph (sentences 4 through 7) does not support the writer's argument and should be deleted?
options: Sentence 4
Sentence 5
Sentence 6
Sentence 7
questions.explanation: The paragraph argues that a skate park would be safer than a parking lot. When skateboarding joined the Olympics does not support that point.

questions.stem: Which revision of sentence 3 states the writer's claim most clearly?
options: Skateboarding is a sport that many people enjoy.
Some people like skateboarding and some do not.
Skateboarders need a better place to go, maybe.
Our town should build a public skate park.
questions.explanation: The essay argues for a skate park, so the claim should name it. "A better place to go" never says what the writer wants built.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 10 to support the idea that a skate park would help businesses. Which sentence is best?
options: Many skaters learn new tricks by watching online videos.
Skateboards can be expensive to buy and to repair.
A busy park brings visitors who shop and eat nearby.
The grocery store has a large parking lot near the street.
questions.explanation: The paragraph argues that the park would help businesses, and regular visitors who shop and eat nearby support that. The other sentences do not.

questions.stem:
Choose the best revision of sentence 13 to conclude the essay.

(13) [[1]]
blanks: That is all I have to say about the skate park idea.
Skateboarding is fun, and that is the reason why I like it so much.
A skate park would make our streets safer and our town busier.
A skate park is a good idea.
questions.explanation: The conclusion should restate the claim and its reasons: safety and help for local businesses. The other choices are vague or off topic.

questions.stem:
Choose the revision that makes sentence 12 parallel.

(12) The city could apply for grants that help towns build parks, and local businesses [[1]].
questions.explanation: Both halves should have a subject followed by "could" and a verb: the city could apply, businesses could sponsor. The other choices break the pattern.

questions.stem: What is the most effective way to combine sentences 5 and 6?
options: Skating in a parking lot means dodging cars and shoppers, in a park, skaters could practice on smooth ramps.
Skating in a parking lot means dodging cars and shoppers, but in a park, skaters could practice on smooth ramps.
Skating in a parking lot, in a park, means dodging cars and shoppers on smooth ramps that skaters could practice on.
Skating in a parking lot means dodging cars and shoppers, and so in a park, skaters could practice on smooth ramps.
questions.explanation: "But" shows the contrast between the parking lot and the park. A comma alone is a comma splice, and "and so" wrongly makes the park a result.

questions.stem:
Choose the revision of sentence 9 that best fits the serious tone of the essay.

(9) The grocery store would no longer have [[1]] in its lot.
questions.explanation: "Skaters practicing" is precise and fits a persuasive essay meant for city leaders. "Messing around" and "goofing off" are casual and undercut the writer's point that skating is a sport.

questions.stem:
Choose the most effective way to combine sentences 3 and 4.

[[1]]
blanks: Rain hit the windows, and it was loud and noisy.
Rain hit the windows, it was loud.
questions.explanation: "Loudly" turns sentence 4 into one word that describes the rain, which is concise and correct. A comma between two sentences creates a comma splice.

questions.stem:
Choose the most vivid verb for sentence 2.

(2) Marisol and her little brother Teo [[1]] on the living room floor with a flashlight between them.
questions.explanation: "Huddled" shows the children crouched close together in fear, which fits the storm. "Sat" and "were" tell nothing about how they felt.

questions.stem: What is the most effective way to combine sentences 13 and 14?
options: The storm ended, and also, Marisol felt proud.
When the storm ended, Marisol felt proud.
The storm ended Marisol felt proud of it.
The storm ended, Marisol felt proud.
questions.explanation: Making the first sentence a "when" clause joins the ideas correctly and shows the timing. The other choices create a comma splice, wordiness or a run-on.

questions.stem:
The writer wants to replace sentence 7 with a sentence that shows Marisol's feelings more precisely. Choose the best revision.

(7) [[1]]
blanks: Marisol didn't know what to do at first.
Marisol was not sure about the thing.
Marisol's hands shook on the flashlight.
Marisol felt some kind of feeling about it.
questions.explanation: Shaking hands show her fear through a specific detail. The other choices tell the feeling vaguely or not at all.

questions.stem: Which sentence could best be added after sentence 5 to build suspense?
options: Teo was five years old and liked dinosaurs.
Marisol's favorite color was green.
Outside, a tree branch cracked and fell.
Their house had three bedrooms and a garage.
questions.explanation: A cracking branch adds tension to the storm scene. The other details do not build suspense.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add a detail after sentence 11 that connects the story Marisol tells to her own situation. Which sentence is best?
options: In the story, the bird kept going for its little ones.
The batteries in the flashlight were almost brand new.
Marisol's grandmother lived in another state.
Birds can fly long distances during migration.
questions.explanation: A bird that keeps going for its little ones mirrors Marisol caring for Teo during the storm. The other details do not connect the story to her.

questions.stem:
Choose the best transition to begin sentence 15.

(15) [[1]] when their parents finally came home, they found both children asleep on the floor.
questions.explanation: The final sentence jumps ahead in time, so "Hours later" signals the shift. "For example" and "In contrast" signal the wrong relationship.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct verb for sentence 6.

(6) Facial expressions and the direction of your hands [[1]] the meaning of a sign.
questions.explanation: The compound subject "facial expressions and the direction" is plural, so it takes the plural verb "change."

questions.stem:
Choose the correct pronoun for sentence 7.

(7) My brother and [[1]] practiced every night at the dinner table.
questions.explanation: The pronoun is part of the subject of "practiced," so the subject form "I" is correct. Drop "My brother and" to test it: "I practiced," not "me practiced."

questions.stem: What is the correct way to write sentence 12?
options: Last month she corrected my sign for butterfly she laughed when I got it wrong.
Last month she corrected my sign for butterfly, and she laughed when I got it wrong.
Last month she corrected my sign for butterfly, and laughed, when I got it so wrong.
Last month she corrected my sign for butterfly, she laughed when I got it wrong.
questions.explanation: The original joins two sentences with only a comma. Adding "and" after the comma fixes the comma splice; removing the comma makes a run-on.

questions.stem:
Choose the verb form that keeps sentence 8 parallel.

(8) The hardest part was learning to watch instead of [[1]].
questions.explanation: After "instead of," the verb takes the -ing form: learning to watch instead of listening. "Instead of listen" is not standard English.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct spelling for sentence 14.

(14) I am still learning the alphabet of a [[1]] that has changed my family.
questions.explanation: Language is spelled l-a-n-g-u-a-g-e.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct punctuation for sentence 4.

(4) Our teacher, a woman named Mrs. Okafor[[1]] came to my aunt's house every Tuesday evening.
questions.explanation: "A woman named Mrs. Okafor" renames "our teacher," so it is set off by a pair of commas.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct way to write the name of the language in sentence 1.

(1) When my cousin Lily was born deaf, my whole family decided to learn [[1]].
questions.explanation: American Sign Language is the name of a language, so each word is capitalized.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct way to write sentence 13.

(13) [[1]]
blanks: The Westside Library has served this neighborhood for fifty years it should keep serving everyone.
The Westside Library has served this neighborhood. For fifty more years it should keep on serving everyone.
The Westside Library has served this neighborhood for fifty years, it should keep serving everyone.
The Westside Library has served this neighborhood for fifty years, and it should keep serving everyone.
questions.explanation: The original runs two sentences together. A comma and "and" join them correctly; a comma alone makes a comma splice, and breaking the sentence after "neighborhood" changes the meaning.

questions.stem:
Choose the verb that agrees with the subject in sentence 2.

(2) The library board [[1]] the change will save money.
questions.explanation: "The library board" is a singular subject, so it takes the singular verb "says."

questions.stem: Which revision of sentence 6 uses the active voice?
options: Saturday is the only full day that the computers may be used by them.
Saturday is the only full day on which the computers are used by them.
The computers can be used by them only on Saturday, the one full day.
Saturday is the only full day they can use the computers.
questions.explanation: In the active voice the students are the subject and do the action: they can use the computers. The other choices keep the passive "be used by them."

questions.stem:
Choose the verb that agrees with its subject in sentence 3.

(3) However, the change will hurt the students and working families who [[1]] on the library the most.
questions.explanation: "Who" refers to the plural "students and working families," so the verb must be plural: depend.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct way to write the word that belongs in sentence 7.

(7) Last year, [[1]] used the Saturday computer lab more than any other group.
questions.explanation: The sentence needs a plural noun, not a possessive, so no apostrophe is used: students.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct way to write the word that belongs in sentence 10.

(10) Without [[1]] hours, those families will have nowhere to go.
questions.explanation: Days of the week are proper nouns and are capitalized.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct punctuation for sentence 12.

(12) For [[1]] the library could close an hour earlier on Mondays, when fewer people visit.
questions.explanation: An introductory phrase such as "For example" is followed by a comma.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct word for sentence 9.

(9) Many of them can only bring [[1]] children to story time on weekends.
questions.explanation: "Their" shows that the children belong to the parents. "There" names a place and "they're" means "they are."

questions.stem:
Choose the correct verb for sentence 6.

(6) Some seeds sprout the next year, but others wait several years before they [[1]].
questions.explanation: The pronoun "they" refers to the plural "others," so it takes the plural verb "grow."

questions.stem: What is the best way to correct sentences 12 and 13?
options: They need so little care, they are a favorite of gardeners who want to plant native flowers.
Because they need so little care, they are a favorite of gardeners who want to plant native flowers.
Because they need so little care; they are a favorite of gardeners who want to plant native flowers.
Because they need so little care. They are a favorite of gardeners who want to plant native flowers.
questions.explanation: Sentence 12 is a dependent clause standing alone, a fragment. Joining it to sentence 13 with a comma makes a complete sentence; a semicolon cannot follow a dependent clause.

questions.stem: Which revision of sentence 2 uses the active voice?
options: The bluebonnet had been named in 1901 as the state flower.
The bluebonnet was named the state flower by Texas in 1901.
In 1901, the state flower of Texas was named to be the bluebonnet.
Texas named the bluebonnet its state flower in 1901.
questions.explanation: In the active voice the subject, Texas, does the naming. The other choices use passive forms such as "was named."

questions.stem:
Choose the correct punctuation for sentence 11.

(11) Bluebonnets need three things to [[1]] sunlight, well-drained soil, and very little fertilizer.
questions.explanation: A colon introduces a list after a complete sentence: "Bluebonnets need three things to thrive" is complete, so the colon fits. A comma there creates a confusing series.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct punctuation for sentence 3.

(3) Bluebonnets are a kind of [[1]] a plant in the pea family.
questions.explanation: "A plant in the pea family" renames lupine, so a comma sets it off. A semicolon must be followed by a complete sentence, and a period leaves the phrase as a fragment.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct way to write the name of the region in sentence 9.

(9) Each spring, families travel to the [[1]] to take photographs in fields of bluebonnets.
questions.explanation: The Hill Country is the name of a particular region of Texas, so both words are capitalized, like the Panhandle or the Gulf Coast.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct spelling for sentence 7.

(7) This helps the plant [[1]] droughts.
questions.explanation: Survive is spelled s-u-r-v-i-v-e.
